For its first ten hours, Wildermyth is charming and great. But, like the Wizard of Oz, once you've played enough to "see behind the curtains" into the game's narrative and gameplay systems, the magic and charm swiftly atrophy. Wildermyth is, ultimately, wildly overrated. I have a piece of advice I often tell my creative writing students: "If a detail is important enough to put in once, it's good enough to bring up again." If, when introducing a character, you spend several paragraphs describing the tattoos covering her body, then those tattoos should be a pivotal aspect of her character. They should be brought up again later by the character herself or others. You do this because it trains the reader to pay attention; it imbues even mundane observations with intrigue. This is, in fact, a form of Chekhov's Gun, from the famous playwright Anton Chekhov who said: "If in the first act you have hung a pistol on the wall, then in the following act it should be fired. Otherwise don't put it there." Wildermyth, however, repeatedly hangs pistols on walls, only to completely ignore them later. For example, one of my primary characters that I've used across all my campaigns is a warrior with a WOLF HEAD. You would think, perhaps, that this might constitute a rather conspicuous detail. You might think other characters that she recruits would ask, "Uh why in the world do you have a wolf head?" But you would be wrong. My character having a wolf head didn't change anything in the story whatsoever. Because Wildermyth's individual story hooks and vignettes are largely self-contained. So a given story arc might have multiple parts that span several chapters, but story arcs never (that I saw) interact with each other. So actual character and world development feels random and disconnected, and as a result I found Wildermyth's story-telling to be uninteresting and emotionless. Sure your characters can "fall in love" but all that really means is some tag in the UI, with minor gameplay and story effects. A sad definition of love, if you ask me. Which leaves us with the game itself, the mechanics. And what's there is decent... but there isn't much there. I have this term - "indie threadbare effect" - that I find myself using all the time, to describe indie games which push replayability far beyond the game's mechanical depth and breadth. That also describes Wildermyth quite well. There's 8 or so scripted campaigns, as well as the choice to pursue a procedural campaign. Your characters within these campaigns can become legacy heroes that can be re-used in other campaigns and even advanced to higher tiers. So it looks like there's a lot of replayability. But the game's mechanical content lasts about 2 campaigns. There are THREE classes, each with 10-15 abilities (passive and active) as well as a small pool of general abilities. There's also 10-15 spells total for the mage class. By the time you've completed your second, maybe third, campaign, you'll have seen and done it all. Of course every person's sense of novelty is different... but I was shocked at how quickly the gameplay grew stale. By the third campaign, it's fair to say that 99% of the battles were mechanically identical to ones I'd already fought before. And even the procedurally chosen mini-vignettes started frequently repeating. The game has an undeniable charm but at this stage, I'd say it's more of a platform than anything. It desperately needs more content. More classes, more abilities, more vignettes. But while all of that will improve the GAME part of Wildermyth, I'm not sure anything will fix its fundamentally flawed story-telling. In a good story, details need to matter. If my main character's head gets replaced with a WOLF SNOUT, that should matter. It should inform every future interaction that character has. But in Wildermyth details don't matter. In short, Wildermyth is just a very light game. Story-lite, gameplay-lite. It's quite breezy. Which may be just what some people want. But anyone interested in depth in their gameplay and story will want to look elsewhere.

This game is praised by other for its randomly-generated storytelling, but the problem is you can’t tell a GOOD story with procedurally-generated sentences that are randomly strung together. A good story involves continuity. If a theme or element is introduced, it should be reinforced and expanded upon later. For example, if a character is a talented musician, it’s a part of their backstory; it’s part of how they cope with adventuring; it affects how other people see them. And over the course of the story, there should be times where that unique trait can be used to solve problems or get them into trouble. That’s DnD roleplaying 101. (I only bring this other because other people praise Wildermyth for being like DnD roleplaying.) Instead, the game generates random elements and then forgets them. In the epilogue, one of my characters “helped So-and-so design cloaks reminiscent of Cape Hook.” This character at no point in the entire game was ever shown to have an interest in fashion, have any connection to random location “Cape Hook”, or have any connection to the person she was helping. It was just madlib where three random nouns were inserted into a pre-written sentence. Unfortunately, that’s how all the story events play out. There are character parameters that guide the madlib selection—a “brash” character will pull madlibs from the “brash” bucket—but they still end up with a series of unrelated scenes. There’s no sense of continuity or climactic progression. On the gameplay front, the tactics-style battles are simple but enjoyable. After 5 hours, they’re starting to feel repetitive, but people have different tastes in terms of complexity. The overworld map gameplay, on the other hand, is paper-thin. There’s just…nothing there. Because of the way “work” towards scouting/building is calculated, the best strategy is simply to group your main squad together and march to the goal, scouting, building, and fighting as a group everything in your path.

I tried my best to like this game, playing through the tutorial and a five-chapter story campaign. Unfortunately I found the writing, which is the most important part, to be underwhelming. People compare this game to XCOM but there is very little in common. This game is all about the story. Things like stats, gear, combat, tactics are an afterthought, seemingly by design. That is fine on its own. The game starts with detailed character creation where you customize not only stats/appearance, but also personality. The game features short segments for every encounter/plot where your characters interact and talk. Their personality influences what they say and do, while the player gets to steer the plot a bit. From a glance this sounds awesome. The problem is that the various character interactions and events come out of the blue. Two characters suddenly have a moment while travelling, and now they're in a relationship (after never having talked before). Two other characters become rivals all of a sudden. Some event comes up and they talk like they've known each other for years, after having been in two fights together. The game expects you to "fill in the blanks" between the story vignettes. It's a game of head-canon. In games like XCOM or Darkest Dungeon where you witness the characters fight through many gruelling missions, you would happily establish the head-canon on your own, shipping your favorite characters etc. Here there is not enough "game" for that head-canon to develop, at least not for me. Each chapter features 5-8 combats which occur over a timespan of several years (??). Then at the end of each chapter you skip another 10 years (?????). I did not find myself feeling much attachment or interest in the characters because I hardly got to see them do anything. It's like the game gave me tiny slivers of insight into what happened during all those years, and expected me to fill in the blanks. I'm sure many people are into that sort of thing, but for me it felt shallow. By the very end you start to have some interest in your characters, but then they retire because each chapter skips 10 years and they get old. The game even features your characters having children, who eventually join the party, but if I was not yet invested in their parents, then how does adding more characters to the mix help? Another major flaw is that the dialogue is all sorts of weird. The characters all talk in a similar fashion, with different coats of paint depending on if they're grumpy or friendly or funny. Everyone speaks in a jarring, short, slightly snarky tone at all times. Start sentences abrupt. Like something you'd find in twitter posts or online dating profiles. They all sound the same after a little while. Then they have kids and the kids also sound the same. When the game switches from your characters to NPCs/plot events, it instead becomes very verbose and prosaic, to the point where it almost feels pretentious. I'm sure the writing would feel more impactful if there was more time spent in building up the characters or plot encounters. As it stands, things go by so quickly that I barely follow the story along because it does not seem interesting enough. Overall, I think this game is good if you really just want a blank slate to fill in. For those looking for a game with more "meat on the bones", whether in gameplay or in story, I would not recommend it.

My first run through the first (tutorial) campaign was a blast. I enjoyed the cheeky writing and the sometimes heartfelt moments. It felt like I was reading some of the old web-comics I used to enjoy. I had moments of sorrow and loss, and moments of triumph. I felt things, and this was good. I also enjoyed the combat mechanics at first which seem to heavily favor mindful positioning and well... not much else. Yes, after about ten hours everything seems to blur into one homogeneous, dull shade. Combat loops are essentially the same for every battle and every class (of which there are three). Classes do not change hardly at all from play-through to play-through because there are only a small handful of potential abilities to choose from on level up. So maybe three main archetypes per class (and that is being very generous). Dialogue and banter remains recycled through every campaign. I expected to discover new story arcs on subsequent campaigns but I found maybe three I hadn't experienced in the first 8 hours later on. (Mainly pet and transformation arcs.) Every character is essentially the same personality. The Legacy system ultimately therefore adds nothing of import to the game. Every character can be boiled down to a handful of dice rolls. So, no, I do not recommend this game at it's current asking price. I have spent 16 hours in game at the moment and I feel I have played it to absolute death. The heart is there but the guts just ain't.

Saying anything negative about this game feels a little bit like kicking a puppy. It's pretty and it wants to be liked so much. But it is dull -- devastatingly banal, completely bland, utterly uninteresting, with characters who can scarcely be distinguished from each other and action that meanders along until you fall asleep. When I stop playing a game, it's usually because I dislike it. I don't dislike Wildermyth. I stopped playing it because there was nothing about it that made any mark on my memory, because it faded from my consciousness almost instantly after I left the game. It was like a glass of water with a teaspoon of brandy in it.

Rolled into the first Gorgon campaign with no idea what I was doing. Wound up recruiting a warrior within the first chapter and I intended on making her a tank with a shield. Her name was Falula. At the end of the first chapter, as we fight the first of what would be many gorgons throughout the campaign, I messed up and she got maimed. Her shield hand was turned to stone. I lived with it, begrudgingly. I kept her in my party for the next several hours of the campaign. She couldn't wield a shield anymore, but she could still fight, and as it turns out, fight well. I made her a Paladin which had the passive of putting her into a "Guardian" stance after every one of her turns regardless of action. This meant that she'd attack the first enemy that walked by her. She held her own throughout several hours of play, pulled her own weight, and as I entered the last fight of the campaign against the Gorgon leader I rewarded her reliability and invested my resources into giving her the strongest one-handed mace I could craft. The final fight was long with many, many enemies. But finally as we're fighting the big boss man himself, as he walks into range to finish off one of my other party members Falula's Guardian procs and she strikes the ugly creature with a crit of the level 3 mace I had just given her. It was just enough to finish him off and so the day was saved. At the end of each campaign you can choose to carry over one character as a legacy character to other campaigns. I could have chosen any of the 5 other able-bodied characters I had. But I chose my stone-handed battle priestess Falula. This game rocks.

Wildermyth is just so good. I'm devoted to trying to get 100% achievements so I've been reading the wiki and planning my party compositions more, and normally that kind of kills the mystique of a game but I'm just stunned by the amount of content I'm still finding, as well as how well all the game's  systems overlap to create something far greater than the sum of its parts. Fundamentally the gameplay loop is extremely well designed, you start with a party of heroes who grow older through the campaign. Campaigns last between 30 and 65 years, and are split between a campaign map and individual missions, a lot like XCOM. Your heroes collect gear, experience, and learn new abilities, but they also grow older and become weaker as a result of their age. Unlike in XCOM or a more traditional CRPG where you tend to get a few good dudes that are indispensable to the party and carry you through a campaign Wildermyth has your heroes gradually become slower and less capable until grandpa finally decides to lay down the giant magic ice sword and retire. Progressing through a campaign lets you try lots of different mechanics, recruit lots of different heroes, you can have highs and lows and the economic systems in the game are just complicated enough that you have good reason to use all the tools at your disposal without any one playstyle becoming overly dominant. It stays fun on multiple playthroughs because the combat is very well made and creates interesting situations, and the overworld is the same. The story told by the mechanics alone is good, but the game is also extremely well written. The sense of lineage and personality that these heroes get throughout their lives is really incredible, there's more than a dozen personality types which each hero has varying amounts of, and the types of people your heroes are determine both what kinds of events and situations you get, as well as what outcomes are feasible in these events. On top of this each hero gets 3 "hooks" which are literal story hooks for a wide variety of personal quests or "opportunities' as the game calls them, these events are everything from simple whimsical asides that offer slight buffs, to characters making peace with their inner demon and becoming part shadow creature. I'm on my 12th campaign at this point and I'm still finding new outcomes or even events I've never seen before. There's certainly repetition, but because there's multiple (sometimes extremely different) outcomes for most of these events it keeps it fresh, and sometimes it is nice when you get an event you know and you know the outcome you want as well, you can just hit F to skip all the way to the choice and if you don’t remember they’ve embedded links to the wiki in the game so you can read all the possible outcomes and pick the one you want. This is a REALLY nice feature if you’ve got a completionist mindset. If you’re like me you probably don’t customize characters at the start of a game in something like XCOM, you wait until someone makes a name for themselves and maybe you give them a cheeky nickname or some cooler looking armour. I had a character I wasn’t very fond of, a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ wizard who I didn’t use much  so he was permanently underleveled, and his name was Bolo. I renamed him Bozo, and then Bozo had a warrior kid who I named Bozo Jr. Jr has been extremely useful ever since and more than made up for their father. Jr is a high mobility warrior with good action economy who’s head was transformed into a crow’s head after they insulted a weird bird lady they met in a barn. I love that. Wildermyth is good at making these narrative arcs, and since you can import characters from other campaigns as legacy characters into new campaigns they end up with this sort of mythic lore that follows them around, the last time I recruited Bozo Jr they got an introduction as a local badass who managed to 1v1 a gorgon and save their town, which is a special introduction that only legacy heroes get. It really is the little things that add up. I’d like to ramble about the characters I’ve made while playing, but that just brings me back to how good the writing is overall. Theres 5 enemy types; mechanoids, cultists, magic bugs, lizard men, and sea/forest monsters. Each of them get their own campaigns, all of which are pretty good. The first two campaigns are simple and light stories, decently told with mechanics that tie the narrative into the gameplay, but the third campaign takes it up a notch by gradually giving you procedurally generated characters who are related to the characters in the narrative, building up to what feels like a important conflict with history and consequences for the randomly generated party you’ve created. It is an excellent integration of narrative and gameplay, and the world it builds feels genuinely magical. Another campaign sees you making choices for and occasionally playing as the primary antagonist, who is themselves a tragic figure that the player is brought into conflict with through realistic and dare I say gripping narrative. The lizard people want to build their own nation and that demands conquering human lands, the player has no choice but to oppose this as the other option would be subjugation. Its a surprisingly deep story about generational conflict. The characters who start that campaign will likely age out by the 5th act, by the end of that campaign everyone is fighting everyone else’s children for the same reason their parents fought. A bittersweet end to a tragic tale, in a game that doesn’t even have animation. I really cannot recommend this game enough. Each campaign takes 4-8 hours to beat but can be played in bite sized increments, the combat is challenging and complex if you want it to be, it is one of the best gaming experiences I’ve had in terms of emergent narrative while also scratching that itch for a tricky turn based squad combat strategy game. Its like fantasy XCOM with more personality.

Started a campaign. I had 4 people in a company together. over 10 years. Two were romantic and the other two were only friends. At the end of the first chapter, the final battle saw the two who were romantic killed in battle. 20 Year Timeskip happens at the end of the chapter thanks to a mod put out by the developers that allow large jumps. At the start of the next chapter, I suddenly have 2 new people in my group.  I was confused, but assumed it was the game just automatically balancing things back so I didn't have only 2 people in my company. I was wrong.  I checked their histories first, saw nothing special.  I checked their relationships after. They both were in their early twenties. They had listed parents. They were the orphaned twins of my two dead company members, having been only 3 years old when they died. The game wasn't 'balancing' to fit the style.  It was throwing me a curveball that made me happy I built two shrines after that bloody battle.  And now I have two orphaned fighters who were most likely raised by the other 2 people in the company due to their comrades dying. This game is unreal.

Early Access Review This game was absolutely spellbinding for my first playthrough... but then it very quickly started to get old, after that. If you are reading through all of these reviews, looking to understand this game, you have probably noticed a theme, by now: Originally posted by Literally Everyone : All of the events started to repeat themselves, really quickly, and it diminished/ruined the fun, for me. I don't want to just repeat this line that has been written a hundred times here, by now, but it basically sums up the biggest flaw with this game. So instead, I'll try to elaborate on the mechanics of WIldermyth a little so you can understand why everyone keeps saying this, and why it's such a problem. As a turn-based RPG, this game is passable; not fantastic , but good enough that you won't get bored of it right away even though it probably couldn't carry the game entirely on its own. What makes Wildermyth unique and fun is the storytelling mechanic, which draws on elements from your playthrough to generate a unique story for your characters, each time you start a new campaign. Characters are generated with a random assortment of personality traits, like cowardice, leadership, bookishness, goofiness, darkness, optomism, etc; I think there are about twenty five of them in all, and they are all given scores between 1 and 100. They generate relationships with one another based on how they met and how compatible their personalities are (friend, rival, lover, parent, sibling) which are rated from 1 to 5 based on how long they have known each other and how closely they have worked together in that time. They have histories that track what sort of experiences they have had, and they have "hooks" which define the sorts of things that appeal to them and can draw their interests. And of course, you have their age and how long they have been involved in the campaign. All of these things are used to generate the storyline. Between each battle the game will check all of the above info for the party that is about to participate in the next fight (your heroes will split up and reform with different groups at different times in the game; they'll be around different people at different times in the story) and it will select an event from a long list of compatible events. For example: if a parent and their child finish a fight together, and the child is more serious than the parent, you may get an event in which the parent laments that their child does not call them "mom"/"dad" anymore. If you have two goofoffs in the same party, and one serious one, they may get into a conflict because the two keep f.ucking around and get the party in trouble, and that third guy won't stand for it anymore. If two rivals have high gambling traits, they might enter a wager concerning the next fight, which only one of them can win and which distracts from the quest. These events are told through comic strips that partly generate the dialogue based on the personality of the characters involved, and may prompt the player to make decisions or attribute checks. The problem with this, is that you never really know, the first time, how much of this is fixed and how much is based on your characters. It is easy to suspend your disbelief and get invested in your characters, the first time, but once you start seeing them again on your second campaign, the paint starts to chip and you lose that magic. Then, you're just playing a somewhat below-average TBS game and you can't ever get that wonderment back from the first playthrough, again. There isn't nearly enough content, here, for the gimmick to work more than once and it is clearly meant to be played over and over again. The legacy mechanics make that clear. BUT... the game is still in early access, lot's more content has been promised, and the devs are pretty regularly updating it on a roughly twice-montly basis, adding new events with every patch. For that reason, it gets a thumbs up from me. My first playthrough, as I said, was spellbinding . I still remember my first party, and their stories, and even when I started to see the strings I still stuck around to play through the rest of the available campaigns (there are three, two more coming later). My second run was almost as good as my first, and it wasn't until the last campaign that I started to feel weary of it. That only happened because I had seen all of the events; the new stuff came too far apart for me to really feel invested in the characters anymore, and without the main gimmick the remainder of the game couldn't hold my attention well enough. If the game looks fun to you, then I would wager that it almost certainly is. But you're only going to get about 5-10 hours out of it, in it's current state, before you lose that. If you really want to get 30-50 hours out of this game, then you should just wishlist it and wait till it comes out of early access. As for me, I'm going to put it away now, and come back to it in a year or two when I have forgotten all of the specific events, so I can play through the two upcoming campaigns from a fresh perspective, again.

It is hard for me to really articulate what makes this game special. The closest comparison I have to describe it is an AI driven D&D game. While there may be other games it can be compared to I dont have experience with them so I will have to defer to others to comment on the genre. With that preamble let me tell you why I think Wildermyth is incredibly special and deserves your attention and time. The first thing I would say about this game is that you will get back what you put into it. When I first played it I thought the idea was cool, I had a lot of fun and I found some of the story plot lines original, funny, quirky and enjoyable. The second game I played (after the intro campaign) I found some of the same plot lines, hooks and jokes. Pair that with a more difficult campaign where some of my main characters died and it wasnt the experience I was looking forward to have. I was immediately disappointed and put the game away for about 4-5 months. I will tell you why I think that was a misjudgment now. I picked up the game for a little variety about a month back. Now, since my last time I played there have been new campaigns added. I still havent gotten to those new campaigns. I just picked up my last game where I left off after I lost a main character. It became obvious to me as I continued this particular story arch that death of your characters is a major part of this game. The intro story gives you a short campaign where my heroes aged at the end but I was able to complete everything without anyone dying. When this second campaign proved more difficult I was frustrated and angry when a character I put my emotional investment died. As I continued this story now months later I began to realize the scope of the typical campaign outside the intro story. These games occur over several decades. At the end of one season my whole starting party retired because they had become too old to adventure anymore. A natural and organic reality that is true to life. As I worked on bringing the next generation of adventurers into the story it finally clicked and I understood what the devs were making in this game. It is a multi-generational game focused on telling and retelling human stories. The mechanic of any hero dying or going into retirement is what puts them into your legacy and allows them to be drafted (from their young beginning) back into a different game where their personalities can be further fleshed out and they can live again in a new setting. Dying and retirement are going to happen, multiple times. That is the whole point. I started to view the game in this light for the first time and suddenly there was a depth and emotional connection I began to develop with every character that honestly I find difficult to put into words. You will just have to experience it yourself. There is something supremely satisfying in seeing a character of your creation learn, grow, form relationships then age and either retire or die defending their loved ones that is deeply invested in this game and it makes it unique on a level I have never experienced in a game before.. That campaign that I gave up on when I lost a main character? I continued the story. In it two of my original members fell in love, had two children who joined the group then both died in battle defending those children in a moment that honestly brought tears to my eyes as I watched it happen. But instead of being angry or frustrated I felt an incredible satisfaction. It was exactly how they would have wanted to go out. The devs now have my undying devotion. I truly find Wildermyth a masterpiece of game design. It is both simplistic in its art and game mechanics while also as deep in its story telling capability. I have yet to use it but the ability to create your own mods, landscapes and story is incredibly exciting to me. I dont know if I will have time to use it but it makes for a source of endless adventure and gameplay when you include your player base in this fashion. I think it is a brilliant move. Overall I cannot recommend this game more but I do so with just a little bit of hesitancy because I have found it to be incredibly special to me and I dont want anyone to dislike it. So please try it out, and please give it a good chance, unlike I did the first time around. If you do, you wont regret it.

description: About This Game Wildermyth is a character-driven, procedurally-generated tactical RPG. Like the best tabletop roleplaying experiences, Wildermyth gives you choices and answers your every decision with consequences that drive your characters forward. Lead a band of heroes as they grow from reluctant farmers into unique, legendary fighters. Combat unexpected threats and strange monsters across interactive battlefields. Unravel mysteries and share pensive moments in an ever-new fantasy setting that blends hard truths and sacrifice with humor and personal storytelling. Where does your myth lead? Come help us uncover it! Reminiscent of tabletop roleplaying, unique heroes are born in unique settings every game. They age, transform, fall in love, disagree, and make harrowing sacrifices. Each hero brings their own organic history and personality with them, but your choices and combat skills are what decide their paths and outcomes. All heroes die someday… but you get to hold on to your favorites. Reintroduce them in the next adventure, and over many lifetimes the myths you make will form your own legendary pantheon. An Imaginative Papercraft World The Yondering Lands, where the game is set, is a richly layered world populated with hand-painted 2D characters and scenery. We’ve paid loving attention to breaking molds and exploring new ideas: no orcs, elves, or goblins here—but watch out for the telepathic insect-dragons and the clockwork undead. Extreme Character Depth Each of your heroes has their own unique generated history, personality, and appearance, and will form relationships with your other heroes. All of these elements change and develop over the course of a playthrough, as characters age, encounter mysteries, and overcome challenges. Choices That Matter Your hero may choose to trust the enigmatic wolf god, leading to a hair-raising change in their appearance and combat abilities. Or they may pursue a romance with a fellow hero, giving each of them a shared buff and more story opportunities. Encounters and events have permanent, character-defining effects, letting you craft the arc of each character. A New Approach to Death Did your favorite character get one-shotted by a tentacled horror-bear? Choose to let a hero "fall back" with a maiming that will lead to some transformative new paths in their legend, or let them go out in a blaze of glory to be remembered for generations to come. Deep and Creative Tactical Combat Combat in Wildermyth emphasizes teamwork and careful positioning, as well as imaginative use of your evolving capabilities and surroundings. Walling and Flanking mechanics provide clear but conflicting incentives, while mystical interfusion lets you remake the battlefield with explosive magic. Multiple difficulty levels mean you can get as intense as you want to. Cooperative Multiplayer In a multiplayer game, you and your friends can each customize and control your own heroes as you play through a campaign. Recommended for up to five players—though in a typical campaign, you start with three heroes and pick up the fourth and fifth along the way. We also support Steam Remote Play. Endless Replayability Pick and choose from a huge bank of combat abilities as your heroes level up in each playthrough, and decide whether you prefer offensive or defensive tactics, brute strength, stealth, or magically flinging fire from a nearby lamp into your enemies' faces. Procedural generation gives you new heroes, new enemies, new story events, and new maps every time you play. A Custom Pantheon of Legends You’ll have the freedom to customize hero appearances, names, histories, and more. As time passes, heroes grow old and may retire, or else might fall in combat—and yes, some will survive all the way to the end. You can add your favorite heroes to a roster of legends and call on them again in later playthroughs. Build your own mythologies and share the awe-inspiring might of your heroes with others.

reviews.text: 战役为：三章。难度为：战斗悲剧英雄、大战役冒险者。落子无悔模式。 在最终战役前夕，我一个同伴的儿子的女友死了。她刚拿了三件奇物。 终于来到了这里，我们要杀掉大主母。长达四十年的冒险即将划上句号。 我没有想到无穷无尽的机械淹没了所有人。 只有我带着同伴的儿子逃了出来，我看着四处可见的断肢以及黑红色混合液体。 我让他逃走了。我回头走了进去。 我已不知过去多久。 多亏了少年时期带来的结晶化身体，我如今在这机械的海洋中已坚不可摧，只靠身体本能便能格挡、闪避所有的危险性行为。 我似乎终于明白多年来冒险从未失败的真正原因了。 不是暗影中随时可以穿透敌人的利箭、不是神念滔天操控其他生物的巫术、也不是在火海中七进七出的烈焰之矛， 是我，马克。 我在不知不觉中已经变成了人们口中的传说。 天亮时刻，我杀死了大主母。 浪漫的烈阳之矛'伦梅尔的儿子、暗影中的诗人罗姆诺克的弟子、通天的大地巫师艾尔亚的义子，欧洛斯，成为了往后一百年人们称颂的英雄。 而我早已被人们遗忘。我是木灵拥护的结晶战士，马克。

漫野奇谭是我绝对不会多看的一类游戏，画风傻不拉叽，五彩Q版低龄化惹人厌。但在圣诞促销的某一天晚上，我想起朋友的推荐，随手点开商店页面看了下介绍，觉得说不准是值得一试的游戏，如果所有事情都在意料之中，那人生也没意义了不是？ 几天后，我打完第一个战役，天已经蒙蒙亮了，我坐在电脑前，看着制作人员名单滚动，动画也开始交代英雄们拯救世界后都去干嘛了：有的人成了坟墓，有的人专门给家里修了一张大桌子用来招待老战友，有的跟年轻时一样还是习惯独处，有的人结婚生子....某几个瞬间，画面中闪过英雄们年轻时的说说笑笑，我的思绪也被牵回了自己人生的起点。 小时候，我认为世界是永恒不变的，老树永远保护我放学回家的街道，学校门口永远都有小贩，好兄弟永远都是明天见，下一款游戏永远不一样； 日子就这么一年又一年的过去，多久我才会变成大人呢？三年是多久？十年后是什么样？ 很多个三年过去了，我今年34，渐渐地我开始明白，人体验不到经历以外的事，有一天，街道整修后老树都不见了，某个学期开学后再也没见过熟悉的小贩，那张跟兄弟们的合影几乎是最后一张合影，新发掘的游戏一连好几个都是类似的； 所有那些美好的回忆，只会一直褪色，每一秒都再也没法复制了，儿时我想成为英雄，现在我想留住回忆。漫野奇谭带给我的不只是巧妙的设计和代入感，它提醒我万物都有终点，我们不得不向过去道别，为了心安理得地活下去，不要忘了保持清醒，尊重当下，享受当下。 感谢制作团队把冰冷的代码变成有血有肉的作品 致敬

这游戏挺让我矛盾的，真的。 你的前两三个本或者前十小时的游戏体验是相当完美的。漫野奇谭把跑团中DM向你讲述故事问你如何行动的角色扮演感体现了淋漓尽致，英雄本身不是完人会生病会变异会老去也会牺牲的设定相当有人情味，多样化的人物标签和随机事件也让游戏更有味道。作为一款主打叙事体验的游戏，游戏本身的“轻量化设计”做的尤为出色，战斗系统在沿用了如CRPG般的类DND的回合制走格子战斗规则，同时做了大量轻量化，把原本晦涩难懂的规则职业系统等简化成易于理解易于上手的“青春版”，同时家园养成以及地图探索都做到了既不复杂也不单调，保证了优秀的游玩体验。 如果你把这款游戏当做一款小品级游戏，那游戏本身已经足够好了。但，如果你对它有更高的要求，那么我必须承认，这游戏也有很严重的后期问题。两三个本或十小时的“保鲜期”一过你的游戏体验将会大打折扣，随机事件和标签毕竟有限，等着你的将是大量重复的事件桥段、重复的战斗场景、重复的人物模板，轻量化立刻暴露出游戏的机制深度完全不够深的问题，导致重复的可玩性和乐趣性大幅降低。这对于一个主打随机事件的游戏将是很致命的问题，当随机性变成了重复性，那玩起来感觉就是在刷角色刷事件刷属性，令人昏昏欲睡，毫无乐趣可言了。 也许放下来过段时间再玩又能得到新鲜感，不过这游戏的体验确实令我感到矛盾，我个人觉得这个价格也不算太便宜，我肯定不只想体验十小时的流程，对它有更高的期望值，但我觉得这个游戏也就止步于此，很难到达我的高期望值了。见仁见智吧，我给不了这游戏太高的评价，也觉得不能算得上很多人吹得那么过的“神作”。

I rarely write reviews, but after nearly 1400 hours, Battle Brothers clearly deserves one. I keep finding myself coming back it, and for good reason: it's a gem of a game. To start, there's a TON of artistic character to this game. Its fittingly gritty and cutthroat, as you're the commander of a band of mercenaries in medieval Germany that is really just out to make some coin. The art style is detailed, yet it leaves just enough to let the imagination wander. The sound effects are actually amazing--you can hear the blood splattering on the ground and the crunching of bones in battle. And the music! It's thoughtfully composed with instruments that actually make sense to have in the situation at hand... it's seriously good stuff. Lastly, the writing in this game so perfectly captures the mercenary life, and there's often something unexpected weaved in that gives you a little chuckle. I generally skip a lot of dialog in games, but *never* with Battle Brothers. There is so much thought and effort put into this game, and it shows. And then you have the gameplay. It's a *hard* game that does not pull punches. You'll lose men to bad planning, and even with good planning you'll still lose them to the old gods of rng... A lot. Apart from the difficulty of success, there's tons of detailed strategy involved in building your company, as well as fielding it. Do you field tanks and archers against orcs? What weapons should you use against giant serpents? How do you even fight goblins that net you and proceed to literally throw the kitchen sink at you? As a contributor to the wiki, I guarantee that it will take many playthroughs before you master all the mechanics. In closing, even if you don't count yourself a tactics gamer (I certainly don't!), if you like challenging medieval fantasy games with highly customizable rpg elements, you really ought to try out this gem. At the very least you'll get your money's worth, but who knows? Maybe it will surprise you like it did me, and it will end up being one of your favorite games in your library. Either way, you won't regret it!

Product received for free Please follow United Critics for quality reviews Battle Brothers Review Overview Battle Brothers is a medieval, turn-based strategy game with management elements. This game is clearly inspired by Mount & Blade, which you can see in the way you go about trading, and travelling around the world map. The key difference from the said game is that Battle Brothers doesn’t have real-time combat, which is instead replaced by the turn-based strategy aspect. This is probably the best way to summarize this game. Breakdown Think before you attack Combat in Battle Brothers has been done incredibly well, and this is coming from someone who is very picky about turn based strategy games! You have a variety of warriors, ranging from your standard archers or swordsman to people with pitchforks. You can arrange your team in various formations which have unique features and provide their own boosts. On top of that, each individual character will level up and develop their own perks. As a result, you will easily get attached to certain characters; especially when the lone survivor from a long drawn battle goes on to level up and fight for you in many successful battles. But you better be careful. Your characters love can be lost forever due to some foolish mistakes. Furthermore, There are many enemies with their own unique mechanics. Some of them even delve into the realm of fantasy. For example, you will encounter zombies who can come back to life and some monsters who will consume the dead to become stronger and you better be weary. Finding your golden trade route One of the things that the game clearly take inspiration from M&B is the way trading is done, as well as the town aspect. Each town has its own kind of economy such as mining, farming, fishing etc. As a result, each town will sell certain goods cheaper and will pay more for certain goods. For example, a farming town will sell you food for cheap, but at the same time, it will pay a hefty sum for a mineral or gem. You will quickly pick up on these things and will look to find your own trade route, which will ensure you get maximum profits in no time! It looks a bit...unappealing The aesthetics is the only place I that can give some negative critique to this game. It isn’t the best and will definitely make a few players stay away from the game. However, once you look past the game’s looks and into what the game holds, then you will definitely be pleased with the game. Are you ready to lose endless hours? Battle Brothers will do just that. This is the kind of game you will start playing only to look at the clock later to see that you spent the entire day just playing it! That being said, people who don’t enjoy this kind of game will probably not enjoy this one either as it does not reinvent the wheel. However, this is very good in what it does. I wholeheartedly recommend this game. Definitely worth buying! Rating: 9/10

description: About This Game The world is fractured, and the old empires have turned to dust. The dead rise from their crypts and Greenskin hordes gather in the distance, as bandits roam free and Nobles prepare for war – the people are left with no choice but to turn to  mercenary bands for aid. Battle Brothers is a turn-based tactical RPG where you lead a mercenary company in a procedurally generated world fraught with dangers of all kinds, and plenty of opportunity for fortune and fame. Decide where to go, which contracts to take on, who to hire, and how to equip your growing mercenary band in this sandbox adventure of grit and valor. The procedurally generated maps of Battle Brothers feature bustling cities, wandering beasts, unique points of interest, and the freedom to explore and engage with everything as and when you wish. Travel in real-time across the varied landscapes of the world to visit the settlements and strongholds spread across the realm, offering you everything from respite and rumors at the local tavern to new recruits for your growing band of battle brothers. Visit markets to sell loot and acquire powerful equipment, or speak to the local lord to see what troubles them, and how much they’re willing to pay to have those troubles taken care of. Settlements and Noble Houses will be your primary source of wealth as they offer dynamically generated contracts of varying difficulty to reflect the coin that comes with completing them – will you take on particularly challenging monsters early in your career to secure greater wealth at the risk of losing your starting sellswords, or will you start focused on local bandits and thieves fleeing justice instead? Be warned – no contract is without consequences, and the quests you take on and how you accomplish them will determine your relationships with the various factions of the world as well as your company’s renown and reputation. Seek opportunities beyond contracts and quests to deepen your pockets – from profitable trade among the many cities and settlements to the great riches hidden in the wild. Will you pursue the life of a merchant and seek out optimal trade routes to bolster your wealth, focus on mercenary contracts, or strike out on your own and seek opportunity and loot in the crypts, camps, and ruins that litter the world? Various crises  can ignite and fundamentally reshape the landscape, demanding radically different strategies and offering new opportunities as time goes on – how will you adapt to an evolving political situation, and more powerful adversaries? Nobles may start massive factional wars, the undead may rise up, or Greenskins may launch full-scale invasions of the land. The brutal battlefields of Battle Brothers reward the clever tactician and punish the careless. As you fight intense turn-based tactical battles on battlefields featuring rough terrain, height advantages, and obstacles to use to your advantage, every swing of the blade carries weight. Take on bandits and beasts of all kinds and maul, mangle, and maim your way through combat. An extremely granular approach to equipment introduces reason to vary your formations and loadouts depending on the team you’ve assembled, and the foe you face – the stab of a spear does little against the fleshless skeleton warriors, while the bludgeoning mace will make quick work of them and their armour. But those very same spears work great alongside shields to keep hungry beasts at bay with their extended reach alongside shieldbashes for those who come close. Meanwhile, though a warhammer could make quick work of a heavily armored bandit, using a dagger to cut between gaps in their protection could leave a very valuable piece of armor intact for you to loot and use. Initiative and action points are important factors on any battlefield, but in Battle Brothers, fatigue plays an additional key role as more powerful attacks and abilities are quicker to exhaust your warriors, especially when covered in layers of heavy armor. A tired soldier has less of their repertoire available to them, and with enough fatigue accumulated, even moving proves difficult – every step taken, every arrow fired, and every sword swung comes at a price, and sometimes a lightly armoured warrior with a dagger and a net can do more damage than if they were heavily armoured and swinging around a morning star. Even if the body is willing, the mind may break first – morale is another key factor to manage on the battlefield! If they have little resolve, your own troops may begin to flee under pressure, but most enemies will similarly suffer should momentum swing in your favour. Will you fight cautiously, taking the enemy on one at a time, or will you seek to slaughter them in quick succession in the hopes of triggering a mass rout? A bad injury – whether temporary or permanent – can quickly end a promising career. While the broken arm that severely reduces combat skills can be healed with rest, a broken elbow joint permanently reduces those very same attributes. From collapsed lungs that make a warrior quick to tire to bruised legs and broken knees that make them slow to act, Battle Brothers’ detailed injury system will break your brothers’ bodies, and keep you on your toes. Keep brothers in reserve when in trouble, and  camp and rest to heal over time, but keep in mind that salaries still need to be paid on time and rations are always limited. A mercenary company is nothing without its fighters – your battle brothers come from all walks of life, grow with experience, and provide unique opportunities for an astute commander. Starting with a small band, you will recruit new procedurally-generated hopefuls to grow your company. Ensure your troops are well fed and well paid, train them in a way that best matches their strengths and weaknesses, invest in their equipment to further their capabilities, and use careful tactics to protect your brothers against the many dangers you face. From Retired Soldiers and Crusaders to Beggars and Graverobbers, your recruits’ backgrounds will determine countless factors about them, including their starting gear and attributes and the traits they are likely to develop, while also greatly influencing what events might come to pass as your company goes from contract to contract. Cultists might convert brothers to their faith as Thieves attract unwanted attention from the law, while Monks play peacemaker and prevent multiple Hedge Knights in your party from killing each other in duels – backgrounds will trigger opportunities of their own, and will often mix with others for unique events within your party. When faced with the choice, would you rather hire the highly skilled Adventurous Noble that expects a higher base pay and comes with the high resolve that makes for a good sergeant to rally your troops? Or would you rather bring on a Brawler or Farmhand that, while cheap to keep on, is likely to come with higher health and fatigue and room to learn the art of combat and grow into an ideal front-line warrior? Physical and mental traits further differentiate these individuals, influencing how they may best be used, and potentially changing your plans as new traits develop over time. Athletic warriors are slower to tire, Brutes make better use of certain weapons in melee as they have great skill aiming for the head, and a brother with a Deathwish won’t waver when hurt, often bolstering the mood of his compatriots. Battle Brothers does away with a restrictive class-based system, instead allowing you to develop each warrior according to what you need and what they’re individually suited for. Each brother is an individual with eight attributes, varied backgrounds, and a multitude of traits they either start with or gain over time, and these will determine the roles they best play. Each individual is inclined towards certain attributes, influencing how you might choose to develop them over time, and a detailed perk tree means you can mold these warriors, and your company,  as you like. A middling warrior with the Fast Adaptation perk will increase their hit chances with every miss, and a heavily-armored brother might benefit most from unlocking the Recover skill to quickly reduce accumulated Fatigue – an individual’s role, strengths, and weaknesses can all be influenced by your decisions. Battle Brothers is a turn-based tactical RPG that prioritizes your freedom of choice as a player – from the way you run your company to the people you fight shoulder-to-shoulder with and the adventures you seek, the world is completely open to your choice.  Will you secure a place in history, or will your mercenary company end with a pauper's grave? The decision, the risk, and the reward are all yours.

reviews.text: EDIT: after playing more, I feel like editing my review. I wish there was a neutral button, but I will settle for negative because the game doesn't deserve the absolute praise it gets. If it was the other way, I would score it positive to balance. Battle Brothers has some very good things and some fatal flaws. It is one of those RNG-heavy, grind-heavy games like Darkest Dungeon. I prefer my games to be deterministic, but in all fairness the RNG can be mitigated a bit in this one (taking spears, surrounding the enemy): nevertheless, there will be a time when the enemy marksman will score a critical hit and kill your archer outright. That would not be a problem, if training a replacement wasn't so slow and tedious. Basically, the whole thing goes like this: take a contract, fight a battle, take some losses that may or may not be your fault, then recruit other mercenaries and build them up fighting other battles, till you lose them too and the process starts again. There is very little in the way of permanent perks for you warband, so when you lose people you're basically back to square one. Money is hard to come by even on the middle-tier difficulty, equipment is expensive and you lose it if you retreat leaving people on the ground. A nasty defeat just adds hours of grind to your campaign. You can partially counter that by playing on the lower difficulty level, but that's simply too easy for a veteran strategy player. The higher ones, I don't even think they are more difficult: they are just more tedious and inflict more busywork on you. The turn-based combat system, on the other hand, is very good and has a lot of nuances, and can keep you entertained for a long time. The gritty atmosphere is great, the variation in weapons interesting, so if you don't mind grinding (but be advised, it is really over the top) you'll find this fun. I find this fun occasionally. But I want games to respect my free time and don't force me into loops of repetitive actions because of bad dice rolls.

A lot of the negative reviews came from the game's RNG system. Many people described it as broken, unfair and unbalanced, while there are a lot of others claimed the system was fair, balanced and had been tested to death. You don't need to believe both sides, from my point of view both of them are correct, and you can buy the game and test it by yourself. The most important thing is that you need to feel FUN when you play a game. (I quitted after playing ~100 hours, just because it's not fun anymore) Based on my data, this game's RNG system is not broken, but is unfair. Let me explain: (1) If you have played XCOM, you will find its RNG system is more close to what you expect. But in fact, the XCOM's RNG is skewed toward the player, because this is a balance between player's real world and the virtual game world. Because what players care is only their OWN team. Imaging there are 100 mercenary groups on the map (1 is yours and 99 are game generated) and there are endless monsters to fight. What players want is that they can keep playing the game to the end, and their team be the standing out one, surviving to the last moment. This 100% player's expectancy, in math world, is 1%. You see the gap here? You don't care about other mercenary groups, right? But Battle Brothers treat your team the same as the others, even they are CPU generated. (2) Now run your Excel, type in =RANDARRAY(1000, 100, 1, 100, TRUE). Now you get a table of random numbers. What this means is that you have a 100-face dice, you roll it 1000 times, collect the data, and do this test again, and repeat it 100 times. These are numbers what random numbers should look like. If you roll a 100-face dice 1000 times, you will have a mean of 50, or very close to it, such as 48.82 or 51.29. Very occasionally you will get a mean like 42.37, but this will be very very very uncommon. The deviation from 50, is actually very narrow. If you plot a distribution of these means (you have 100, because you repeat the test 100 times), you will get a "normal distribution", with the center located at 50. (3) Now check the distribution of every number. If you roll a 100-sided dice 1000 times, you can expect that most of the numbers will be rolled 10 times. Some of them may have appeared 9 or 11 times, even 8 or 12 times, but overall they will approach 10. Very occasionally a number may only get rolled 2 times, or luckily 18 times, but this will be uncommon. The distribution of these numbers of "numbers of getting rolled", will also be a "normal distribution". (4) In Excel 2003, the RAND function used the Wichman & Hill algorithm for generating pseudo-random numbers. Starting with Excel 2010, the Mersenne Twister MT19937 (32-bit) algorithm is being used. As you know, the MT system, is used by the RNG system of Battle Brothers. That means, they should be the same. (5) Now record every RNG number in your fights when you play Battle Brothers. You can record only yours, only the enemies, but not both. For RNG calculation, you have a fixed number (that's the hit roll, the final value calculated from the basic hit roll and many modifiers, of your or your enemy's attack) and a random number (randomly generated by the RNG system, to beat the former fixed number). We want the random numbers, not the fixed numbers. In every fight, generally you can record more than 100 values, so 10 fights are enough to make a preliminary conclusion. If you want to do it quickly, you can use Cheat Engine to lock the fatigue and the action points of your brothers, so that you can regenerate these numbers quickly. (6) Do a t-test to see if your distribution can be tell from the Excel distribution. Based on my data, I have a 99.99% confidence to say that these two systems are different. In Battle Brothers, some minor algorithms are applied so the numbers are slightly skewed toward both sides, so that encouraging very lucky and very unlucky events to occur. But this modification, based on my data, applies equally to you and your enemies. (7) But why can a system applying equally to both sides be called unfair? Because in Battle Brothers the developer did not take the factor "weight" into consideration. This makes the game more challenging and this is the base different that distinguish Battle Brothers from XCOM. Things with same incidence do not mean they bear the same weight (or, significance). In business, we call this risk management. For a high-level team, being extremely unlucky versus being extremely lucky bears different weights. The benefit gained from being extremely lucky is minimal. It may result in a battle you originally need 20 turns to beat with some mild to moderate injuries into a battle you beat in 10 turns without any injury. That's nothing. However, the weight of being extremely unluckly is heavy, you may lose an important brother and ruin your whole team. It is, the benefits you get from being extremely lucky, even several times, do not match the weight of ONE single loss of being extremely unlucky. An enemy being extremely unlucky? You don't care, right? But what if an enemy being extremely lucky? The same rule applies here. Why you want to play an unfair game? Because, brothers, the real world is cruel and the same unfair. Fair worlds only exist in dreams and in games. In real world, you don't bear the same weight as those rich people, right? So, you must change your mind when playing Battle Brothers. The game mechanism treats your team the same as any other CPU team. You are going to fail anyway. The soul of Battle Brothers lies in the STORY you build around your team brothers, not lies in beating the game to the end. There is no end in this game, just memories.

I've hesitated to write this review for quite a long time. Despite having a mostly negative opinion about it since its release in 2017, I just couldn't get myself to form it into a review, because... this game actually has A LOT of things going for it: 1) The visuals are rather unique - well-drawn dark fantasy with clearly recognizable classic references and tropes. Actors have multiple layers for wounds, degraded equipment, and gore. World map is clean, clutterless, and strikes a great balance between simultaneously being realistically dull on your mundane trips and exciting when you explore the unmapped corners of the world. 2) The raw amount of content (mercenary backgrounds, equipment, enemies, skills and perks, quests, cataclysms, etc) is very respectable, especially with content DLCs. 3) The overall concept of the game (mercenary band sandbox) is mostly unexplored by the industry - I struggle to name similar games without heavy generalizations (like Mount and Blade, XCOM, Xenonauts, etc). 4) The writing, while being a rather small part of the game, was not neglected, and it really shows. On paper, this game has everything to grab you by the neck and pull you into its world, robbing you of dozens of hours of free time. And it does so for some players (as is shown by 86% of positive reviews at the time of this review). At first and second look, it is a very good game. And it is. It just doesn't click with me (and with a bunch of other strategy lovers, as can be seen in other detailed negative reviews). And since this game is not in dire need of positive reviews, I will leave a negative one as a cautionary tale to other strategy enthusiasts, seeking to scratch the “xcomy” itch. Here it goes. 1) A tale of “BAD RNG” While a majority of short and less detailed negative reviews cite “bad RNG” as a reason for their negative attitude towards the game, I respectfully disagree. True, unadulterated RNG is… neutral. 40% accuracy swing (a rough baseline for most untrained troops in this game) is more likely to miss than hit. Such is math. And missing 3 times in a row, while feeling bad and unfair, has a roughly 22% chance of happening – which is a lot. What makes this RNG “bad” is the lack of instruments to counter bad outcomes. What happens in XCOM, when enemy crits your soldier, leaving him panicked and on low health? Well, you usually have a lot of options to deal with this situation, depending on what you brought to the table – suppressive fire, flashbangs, smoke screens, taunts, destroying enemy’s cover in a gamble to kill him in 1 turn, healing your wounded soldier up to give him a chance to survive another hit. And while not all those tools guarantee you a happy ending, you at least have some say on how the situation proceeds to unfold. What happens in Battle Brothers, when enemy crits your soldier, leaving him panicked and on low health? Well, he probably dies, unless you have the capacity to wrap up the whole engagement in one turn. There is very little you can actually do, once your line is engaged with the enemy. Even if you kill the enemy who caused this, there are usually others next to him, who will either take his place and finish the job or can already attack diagonally from their current position. Roughly speaking, you can: a) clear the whole flank so that nobody can come over and finish off your soldier in one turn, giving him time to retreat – this requires a lot of DPS output which is often either unavailable on low levels or is also necessary elsewhere. b) Use the push\pull actions of some weapons and shields – unreliable (subject to RNG), hinders your damage output and rarely helps - it just postpones the inevitable. c) Use the “swap positions” ability which requires a perk point, spends time and is not available on low levels. It’s not the RNG itself that is or feels bad. It’s the brutal and deterministic helplessness that makes engagements feel bad and unfair. This problem is further exacerbated by: 2) Lack of tactical depth and overwhelming power of meta builds. It’s that simple. 80% of your fights happen in tactically neutral environments (grasslands with small 1-2 tile “hills”), where all you can really do is form a line, exchange ranged attacks and lock in melee combat – while fun for a few fights, this gets old fast and will not change until you start encountering special types of enemies or get Lone Wolf supercombatants in your party. a) Height advantage is nice to have but rarely can be utilized in a meaningful and truly impactful manner unless you fight in the mountains. b) Flanking is usually out of the question – at least in the early game, when you are usually at least matched in numbers with your enemy (and almost never actually outnumber them). This is less true in the late game, when you rock a bigger party and have juiced up dedicated Lone Wolfs that seek isolation on the flanks. c) Other types of terrain don’t bring anything to the table – the average challenge to your tactical genius usually comes down to recognizing an opportunity to force your enemy to fight in shallow water by standing on the neighboring dry tile or finding a way to use a tree and a bush to shorten your frontline. Not terribly exciting. 3) Frontloaded challenge. Issues I described above are, unfortunately, especially painful and obvious at the start of the game. The lack of meaningful instruments to deal with unfavorable RNG outcomes becomes less acute once you get the beefy gear and are less punished by incoming hits. The lack of tactical depth somewhat dissipates once you specialize your soldiers – but the problem of some builds being objectively better then others arises, still somewhat diluting the depth of the game. Problem is – not a lot of players have the stomach to carry on through the hardships to see the game slightly improving down the line. First impressions matter. And I’m pretty sure that there are a lot of players who will never touch this game again because they were brutally burned in the first few hours of gameplay – even if they would otherwise enjoy it at the later stages and would play it for hundreds of hours. And every time I’m trying to get back to this game, I instantly get a harsh reminder of why I stopped playing last time. This is a shame, because the game is otherwise pretty solid. The only other game I have similar feelings about is Darkest Dungeon – which also suffers from the same issues despite being a superb game. All that said, I’m still glad that this game exists and I hope that the next project of this devteam will be a banger. They have all the tools and talent to pull it off, hopefully they got enough experience with BB.

This game is for a very particular type of person, someone who enjoys difficult games that require time and a lot of failure to learn and master. I thought I would be that type of person, but i feel this game loses something along the way, it stops becoming about learning or overcoming a challenge. For the first dozen hours I thought it was about that, but its not. I personally feel battle brothers is about failure, its about losing brothers, getting your face kicked in over and over again and learning you are not top of the food-chain. Full on dwarf fortress "losing is fun" style. A lot of games can do this idea really well, Darkest Dungeon, Kenshi ect. But i feel battle brothers focuses on the wrong aspects of what makes those games fun. I love Kenshi because every time you fail or get beaten down you get stronger and learn, its really about overcoming a challenge and becoming a badass. In battle brothers when you get beaten down you really don't gain very much... you just rebuild and go to the next fight, knowing that all your work could be undone again due to nothing but bad RNG. You can learn little tricks here and there but eventually it all just comes down to how lucky you get. A lot of games have a dependence on RNG but i haven't seen many that rely on it quite as much as battle brothers does. There are plenty of people who don't mind this type of thing and find a lot of enjoyment in this game but if your looking for something else this might not be a fun game for you.

Probably the most conflicted review I have ever written. Darkest Dungeon is one of my favorite games of all time, but Darkest Dungeon 2 is an exhausting experience. What made the first game so enjoyable was its sense of urgency and pacing. It was a thrill to explore a dungeon and leave with your party barely intact, grateful you had survived, or to dominate a run completely with loot to show for your skill. You were in, you were out, and you had a story worth telling. If you were not in the mood for an intense challenge, you could bring strong gear, keep your torch level high, and do the bare minimum for less loot. If you wanted a desperate fight for valuable materials, you could still optimize your gear but take fewer supplies, keep the torches low, and brace yourself for a run that was both punishing and fun. Either way, it was a short but exhilarating rollercoaster. It had its flaws, but the experience was powerful and rewarding when you played well and made the most of your resources. In Darkest Dungeon 2, those dynamics are gone. Runs are long and draining, with a fixed and punishing difficulty curve that can ruin you for a single mistake or a misunderstanding of your heroes’ abilities and quirks. All of your favorite characters return, but they feel weakened. Loot is no longer about the thrill of discovery; it is tied to a fixed currency-based progression or repeating the same mini-boss grind in hopes that he has the trinket you need once you reach them. The only way to influence difficulty is to choose a safer route, but you are still locked into the same drawn-out road toward the inevitable defeat that awaits at the final boss, one you are unlikely to survive if you took the safer path that only rewards you with scraps. Perhaps Red Hook wanted to capture the fatigue of a stagecoach journey through a harsh, oppressive land. But in doing so, they forgot what made the first game exciting. Difficulty and tedium do not have to coexist at the expense of fun.

I wanted to love this game. I loved the first one, and patiently waited for the EGS deal to die and for 1.0 to release. I was wary of the smaller roster, but kept my head in the sand until I played it. I almost wish I hadn't. Almost. With that foreword, I give you... AN EXHAUSTIVE LOOK AT DARKEST DUNGEON 2 THE GOOD The game is beautiful, and the soundtrack, while less memorable, is still good. The iconic 2D style was turned into 3D masterfully, animations and all. The story is solid, but confusingly presented; Only after looking it up was it considerably good. THE HORROR - MECHANICAL MISS DD2 focuses far more on doing hours-long runs of treks to The Mountain than a decent-sized dungeoncrawl, where preparations and planning are thrown out the window entirely. You must slog through, essentially, four DD1 dungeons before reaching the final bossfight of each Act; Do this 5 times, and you win. Many stats, such as PROT and ACC have been repurposed into 1-use 'tokens' that apply to characters, and... It was fine. Not my favorite. Camping is gone, replaced with the 'Inns' after each region. Instead of preparing your camp skills and knowing what it is you can do, you now have to hope and pray that this Inn has what you want. Often, it does not, but the dialogue inside is cool at least. I did not care for the navigational minigame with the carriage and found most Stagecoach items sorely lacking in usefulness. The pancake maker was my favorite. Didn't care for pets, either, but the Shrieker one is cute. Your characters' deaths don't particularly matter, either. Keeping characters often requires an Act boss clear, and there is no combat retreating this time around, meaning it's hard to keep your squad... Oh, and no class dupes. No double HWM, no double Hellion, etc. If you need a Man-at-Arms for your next run but don't want to lose your kept, named one, tough tits. Hero upgrades are, also, per run and not per character. The stress mechanic has been gutted, and can comfortably be ignored. Every negative affliction has been turned into 'Meltdown', which just lowers your health to ~10% and makes people dislike them... and that's it. You can do this as many times as you want in one combat, and there is no Heart Attacks. 'Resolute's do the opposite- Heals, makes people like them. The only unique affliction is Flagellant's TOXIC, which is a boon really, and can help you sweep the game with minimal hassle. Yes, the iconic mechanic of DD1 is gutted and useless, I'm glad you noticed. Remember when I said they abandoned their niche? There's also, paradoxically, a significant focus on per-battle affairs, as getting fully healed after each fight is real easy, despite healstalling being mostly gone (a good thing, I admit). Without caring for the Stress system and everyone getting nearly fully healed after every fight, each run turns into... a horrible slog. In DD1, there was no guarantee of being healed and stress afflictions hampered you significantly. Every fight, even against the same enemies, was different, and is how hundreds of hours were far less stale. And on top of all this, each run can last you up to 3 hours apiece, which is absolute agony to lose at the Act boss. Even in DD1, if you lost a whole team, it was not preceded by a 2 hour slog beforehand... Unless you were trying to one-trip the Crimson Court. And, of course, each run is entirely distinct and disjointed from the one before and after it. Those do not matter, because there's no simple economy to keep up with, just how many Candles you bring back for upgrades that may or may not effect your current roster. The interesting planning of having to do a dangerous Antiquarian money-run or having to skimp out on supplies after a few bad weeks from DD1 is gone. Entirely. On the old road... Where's my Hamlet? The Hamlet is gone, replaced with a different hub. Keeping money and relics is worthless in a run, because they'll be thrown out for a new currency- Candles. These are what upgrade heroes, unlock trinkets & items, let you keep heroes, let you acquire cosmetics, etc. I was not impressed by many of the new DD2 trinkets. There is an extreme obsession with mixing & matching item sets, now with item types rather than 2 exactly paired items, a-la Crimson Court. I didn't find most of them worth a damn though- usually, simple +20% healing is better than some potential debuffs. ROSTER CUTS From DD1, we've lost Abomination, Arbalest, Antiquarian (Though, they're an enemy now), Crusader , Houndmaster, Musketeer, and Shieldbreaker. And we gained... The Runaway. An excuse to show off the new fire DOT. And Flagellant is a unique blight-based hero now. Utterly. Unacceptable. You can't even equip Bounty Hunter at the Crossroads. You have to hire him at an Inn- where, of course, he may or may not be at. He's super good & versatile, of course, but... But why? And why is Flagellant so different? It's not because you only had two characters who can Blight because Abomination & Antiquarian got axed, is it? It's not that I don't want him to be changed, he's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ GREAT in DD2, but... Why ONLY him? It's totally the blight thing. THE INCONSISTENT, HORRIFIC, UNGODLY RELATIONSHIP SYSTEM Oh my GOD this system is hair-pullingly impossible sometimes. All heroes have relationships with one another, gauging how much each of them likes eachother, and the result is entirely, bafflingly random. Heroes aren't assigned different likes or dislikes or flags, such as DD1's 'Religious' flag for camp skills. Instead, every time a choice comes up- Helping people, grabbing trinkets, whether to fight or flee, etc, it's randomly decided who will get along with who. If you don't catch some sour relations early enough, you're in for a Dwarf Fortress tantrum spiral as bitterness begets bitterness and nobody gets along. After resting at an inn with negative enough relations, two characters will become 'Envious' or 'Hateful' with one another, and two skills (one skill each) will DEBUFF the other, sometimes to a HUGE detriment, for the rest of the region. Hope it didn't happen at the Mountain. It's possible to fix these relations with items at an Inn with alcohol, until someone gets the quirk to stop drinking. Hope you unlocked enough Inn items to take care of it! (Which is why early runs will have hateful parties; no unlocked items to remedy it.) You can get positive relations too, and 2 skills will buff each hero, but the transaction isn't equal. Between a MAA and a PD, for instance, the MAA using a Negative skill may give the PD a Taunt & Weakness token, meaning that they'll draw aggro and take a nasty hit. Meanwhile, if they had a positive relationship, the MAA using that same skill would... Heal 1 stress. In a game where Stress doesn't matter. It doesn't help that even if heroes were carried over from a previous run as best friend, they now are strangers and within 10 minutes can be at eachother's throats. Nothing is consistent. A Hellion can help stranded folks out, then a region later, want to rob them. Of all the bad ideas in DD2, THIS one should have STAYED on that whiteboard. And the Bosses? The Lair region bosses were re-used concepts or fairly bland. The Act bosses were unique and tough, but if every boss takes 3 hours to get to, I cannot recommend going in blind just to lose. After all that... Darkest Dungeon 2 is an inferior game to its predecessor. It has taken the beloved niche it carved out and thrown it aside, wanting to become more... generic. It was alarming to find that  the Nameless King from Dark Souls 3, a similar 'hardcore' RPG filtered less people than DD2's 2nd of 5 Act bosses. DkS1's Anor Londo , the halfway point, filters less people. It's no wonder why. Play Darkest Dungeon 1 instead.

I played the Darkest Dungeon series in reverse order. I started with this one, then tried the first. What's desperately lacking from Darkest Dungeon 2 is a more rewarding sense of progression and permanency. The progression in Darkest Dungeon 1 speaks for itself for anyone who has played it - you can suffer setbacks by losing crucial heroes, but you are always gradually progressing forward through hamlet upgrades and growing your hero roster. In Darkest Dungeon 2, there are unlockables that provide small buffs for future runs, but these fall into the common rogue-lite trap of slowly diluting the item pool with so much trash that is never useful. A 5% chance to increase my attack at the beginning of a turn will never be better than the basic bottle of whiskey. Even completing hero stories and unlocking their full move-sets has a downside. You unlock moves you never use, meaning that positive relationships have a larger chance of selecting an unused move to buff. Or, worse, negative relationships select an unused move and force you to use it, thereby restricting your control and frustrating any strategic decisions. When I am drawn to limiting my unlocks as much as possible, there is something fundamentally wrong with the game design. Darkest Dungeon 2 is also easier, but in an unsatisfying way. You will quickly become knowledgeable enough to make it to the final encounter on nearly 100% of runs. But several final bosses require restrictive team compositions (and foreknowledge) to succeed. Even then, some fights come down to RNG (the third confession). Losing a 2-3 hour run at the final boss hurts, because you have to slodge through another 2 hours of easy fights with no risk before you can try again. So the game play loop is using those 2 hours to effectively prepare for the final boss. It just isn't as satisfying as the gradual progression in Darkest Dungeon 1, where each expedition offered risk and reward, even those not involving a boss fight. There's a few other unfortunate setbacks from the design of Darkest Dungeon 1. The worst for me is that you no longer have unique afflictions, like Hopeless, Masochistic, Abusive, Refractured, etc. Each hero in DD1 also had unique barks for each affliction state. These are now completely absent. DD2 has only 'Meltdown', which always has the same effect: it drops your hero to 20% HP and lowers their relationship with the other heroes. This is immediately reversed with a heal and a few bottles of whiskey. Darkest Dungeon 2 is visually gorgeous. The presentation is superb. But after the initial delight provided by the game's aesthetic dulls, the gameplay loop has little staying power. I feel myself being drawn back the original.
