Coming from Darkest Dungeon 1, I was very excited to try out the sequel. I was optimistic about the game and cautiously aware of the fact that the core gameplay loop had changed in the sequel, so I tried to keep an open mind, but unfortunately all I can conclude after playing the game myself + reading more about it afterwards is: I don't find it fun. That doesn't mean it's a bad game, it's simply that I don't enjoy it coming from the original. This review is intended primarily for folks who enjoyed the original Darkest Dungeon, detailing some differences between the original and sequel to help you decide whether the game is worth your purchase. To start off: the artwork, music, and general atmosphere is fantastic and very reminiscent of the original Darkest Dungeon. The core, turn-based strategy element of combat encounters remains the same and carries a similar, punishing weight to the original. Certain combat mechanics have changed, such as base accuracy not existing (always 100%). In fact, all combat mechanics have largely done away with base values and have been replaced by a new combat status effect system called tokens. I.e instead of a hero having "20 base Dodge" and an ability giving a "+25 Dodge" buff, base dodge is non-existent, and instead an ability can add a "Dodge" token to a character that gives a raw 50% chance to dodge the next attack, or "Dodge+" token that gives raw 75% chance to dodge the next attack. Some new tokens like Combo, Blind, Weak, Vulnerable, etc... exist that will be unfamiliar to players coming from DD1. All tokens are represented by an icon below the health bar, which take some time to learn and get familiarized with, but the information is readily available in a menu by pressing C. I personally think this token system is a shining jewel of DD2. It makes combat modifiers much easier to understand and digest, while avoiding the problem present in late game DD1 of soft requiring accuracy buffing trinkets on all heroes in order to land any attacks on monsters in high level dungeons. My main gripe with the game is it's near complete removal of linear progression. There's no Hamlet, consequently there are no Hamlet buildings to upgrade, there's no resolve XP or levels on your heroes, trinkets all disappear at the end of mission, money disappears at the end of a mission, there's no upgrading a hero's weapon, there's no upgrading a hero's armor, there's no upgrading a hero's skills (you can upgrade them 1 level during a mission, then they're reset afterwards), there are no heirlooms (because there's nothing to spend them on), stress is reset to 0 at the end of every mission for all characters which completely removes the aspect of end of mission stress management that's so integral to DDI. The game feels like a mini DDI campaign that would normally consist of weeks of meticulous planning, gold and heirloom management, varied roster building, calculated risk taking for trinket hunting,  multiple ups and downs that all play their part in a grand story, all crammed into a 1-2 hour long, rouge like experience. Once you complete that experience, you run it back. If you're someone who enjoyed the long-term planning associated with DD1, just know that that virtually doesn't exist here. I say "virtually" above because there are some aspects of the game that do persist. E.g new skills can be unlocked for a hero via a "Shrine of Reflection", and those skills will remain unlocked in future runs. These shrines are nodes that will randomly spawn during a mission, and you'll choose one hero to complete a sort of combat mini-game (for some reason? the mini games are trivially easy and more of a chore than a challenge, which contrasts oddly with the typical, high-difficulty identify of Darkest Dungeon) or sometimes simply go through a bit of narration in order to unlock a new skill. The intended narrative aspect here is that the hero is "confronting their past memories" to unlock new skills in their kit, which may be enjoyable for some, but to me feels like an annoying "jump through this hoop" way of getting your hero equipped with the skills you want. It's far different than DD1's take the hero to the guild and spend 800 gold to unlock your desired skill system. While it still allows for full hero skill tree unlocks and consequent skill loadout flexibility in the long run, it takes multiple hours to unlock all skills for a single hero, which puts you 1-dimensional, restricting position of feeling like you should be using the same 4 heroes that you've already spent time unlocking skills for if you want to have a synergistic lineup. There are some other persistent unlocks, such as relics, stagecoach upgrades, and content from the Altar of Hope, but these are more-so improving the baseline of subsequent runs in simple ways as opposed to giving a true feeling of progressing through the game. The stagecoach driving system feels very clunky. Navigating left and right across the path feels like an unresponsive, subway surfer esque mechanic randomly inserted into larger game for no apparent reason. If you're someone coming from DD1, I'd recommend you come into this game with the mindset that this isn't Darkest Dungeon. It's a game with a punishing, turn based strategy combat system similar to DD1 with similar design and atmosphere, but at it's core is a rouge like consisting of multiple 1-2 hour experiences, not one over-arching campaign. The game is largely great when viewed in its own light, just don't expect a general, upgraded version of the original Darkest Dungeon.
IMPORTANT NOTE If you already own DD1, don't make the same mistake I did - buy the Iron Crown bundle and get DD2 for £25. Steam support unfortunately won't refund the difference.

DARKEST DUNGEON 1 PLAYERS PLEASE READ BEFORE PURCHASING DD2 is a fun and approachable standard 3 map rogulite with much of the great art and style of DD1. However, you have to go into this experience with the full understanding that this game is NOTHING LIKE Darkest Dungeon 1. In the first game, there was a steep learning curve as the game punished you over and over again while you tried desperately to keep as many of your characters alive as possible through murky mechanics and unforgiving RNG. Over time, you learn the systems and improve all of your different recovery and gearing locations so that you get your people surviving longer and with better item prep. You got to know the ins and outs, the strength and weaknesses, and the quirks of each of the members of your teams. In the end, weeks... months.... years later, you may get to beat the game. DD2 has none of that. As a standard 3 map roguelite, the whole point of the game now is to charge in and experiment aggressively. Once you get to the farthest inn you think you can make it to, you end the game, collect your candles to invest in the meta game, and get ready to try again; just like every other 3 map roguelike in exsistance. So, this game is faster and more accessible with great art, and interesting story and approach and it has some interesting twists on the standard roguelite, but that is still what you are going to get this time. The irony is, they spent way more time in this game giving each "character" a back story and development, but in the end, there is no development as they just die and come back over and over with extremely limited permanency. You invest absolutely NOTHING in any one character despite the game saying you do. Instead, you are investing in the entire CLASS of character. Each individual means nothing. In the end, if you are looking for a more polished DD1, this is NOT it. If you are looking for a much more normal roguelight set in the same universe as DD1 than you are good to go and will have a blast!

The interesting planning of having to do a dangerous Antiquarian money-run or having to skimp out on supplies after a few bad weeks from DD1 is gone. Entirely. On the old road... Where's my Hamlet? The Hamlet is gone, replaced with a different hub. Keeping money and relics is worthless in a run, because they'll be thrown out for a new currency- Candles. These are what upgrade heroes, unlock trinkets & items, let you keep heroes, let you acquire cosmetics, etc. I was not impressed by many of the new DD2 trinkets. There is an extreme obsession with mixing & matching item sets, now with item types rather than 2 exactly paired items, a-la Crimson Court. I didn't find most of them worth a damn though- usually, simple +20% healing is better than some potential debuffs. ROSTER CUTS From DD1, we've lost Abomination, Arbalest, Antiquarian (Though, they're an enemy now), Crusader , Houndmaster, Musketeer, and Shieldbreaker. And we gained... The Runaway. An excuse to show off the new fire DOT. And Flagellant is a unique blight-based hero now. Utterly. Unacceptable. You can't even equip Bounty Hunter at the Crossroads. You have to hire him at an Inn- where, of course, he may or may not be at. He's super good & versatile, of course, but... But why? And why is Flagellant so different? It's not because you only had two characters who can Blight because Abomination & Antiquarian got axed, is it? It's not that I don't want him to be changed, he's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ GREAT in DD2, but... Why ONLY him? It's totally the blight thing. THE INCONSISTENT, HORRIFIC, UNGODLY RELATIONSHIP SYSTEM Oh my GOD this system is hair-pullingly impossible sometimes. All heroes have relationships with one another, gauging how much each of them likes eachother, and the result is entirely, bafflingly random. Heroes aren't assigned different likes or dislikes or flags, such as DD1's 'Religious' flag for camp skills. Instead, every time a choice comes up- Helping people, grabbing trinkets, whether to fight or flee, etc, it's randomly decided who will get along with who. If you don't catch some sour relations early enough, you're in for a Dwarf Fortress tantrum spiral as bitterness begets bitterness and nobody gets along. After resting at an inn with negative enough relations, two characters will become 'Envious' or 'Hateful' with one another, and two skills (one skill each) will DEBUFF the other, sometimes to a HUGE detriment, for the rest of the region. Hope it didn't happen at the Mountain. It's possible to fix these relations with items at an Inn with alcohol, until someone gets the quirk to stop drinking. Hope you unlocked enough Inn items to take care of it! (Which is why early runs will have hateful parties; no unlocked items to remedy it.) You can get positive relations too, and 2 skills will buff each hero, but the transaction isn't equal. Between a MAA and a PD, for instance, the MAA using a Negative skill may give the PD a Taunt & Weakness token, meaning that they'll draw aggro and take a nasty hit. Meanwhile, if they had a positive relationship, the MAA using that same skill would... Heal 1 stress. In a game where Stress doesn't matter. It doesn't help that even if heroes were carried over from a previous run as best friend, they now are strangers and within 10 minutes can be at eachother's throats. Nothing is consistent. A Hellion can help stranded folks out, then a region later, want to rob them. Of all the bad ideas in DD2, THIS one should have STAYED on that whiteboard. And the Bosses? The Lair region bosses were re-used concepts or fairly bland. The Act bosses were unique and tough, but if every boss takes 3 hours to get to, I cannot recommend going in blind just to lose. After all that... Darkest Dungeon 2 is an inferior game to its predecessor. It has taken the beloved niche it carved out and thrown it aside, wanting to become more... generic. It was alarming to find that  the Nameless King from Dark Souls 3, a similar 'hardcore' RPG filtered less people than DD2's 2nd of 5 Act bosses. DkS1's Anor Londo , the halfway point, filters less people. It's no wonder why. Play Darkest Dungeon 1 instead.

If You Are New To This IP, Welcome, Enjoy The Delightful Suffering With Us. If You Are Fan Of The First One, This Sequel Might Disappoint You. To me Darkest Dungeon 2 is a mixed bag. I am a fan of the original one. The gruesome Gothic artstyle and the superb narration really encapsulate me. The stress and resolve system are both pain in the butt, but frustratingly addicting. It is quite a unique turn-based RPG experience. Now the sequel is out of early access and I jump right into it. Most of the mechanics remain the same, yet many of the features that make the first one stand out, are either lacking or simplified in the sequel. Maybe it is done so to appeal to a wider audience, or maybe the dev shift the focus to something else. I still find the game enjoyable, nonetheless. It's just that the sequel loses what makes the first one so unique. Things I Like About Darkest Dungeon 2: 1. Art, Animation, And Music (I think it's official to call the 3D sequel "Risk Of Rain 2 Treatment".) I hesitant to call the art direction of Darkest Dungeon 2 "improvement" because the original 2D art has its charm. Yet I cannot deny the 3D environment with the same artstyle looks extra lively, the burning city, the swampy rain forest, the misty fishing hamlet, etc. I also like how beautifully animated everything is. From idle animation, to preparing a skill, to executing said skill, to finishing the move, the animation feels so fluent, friends or foes alike. And finally, the music. This, at least, I am confident to say that sequel surpass its predecessor. Something about the melody just sticks with me, even after I have beaten the game. I can still find myself humming the music of traveling stagecoach. 2. Hero Story This one of the new features of the sequel. It basically is the background story of each character narrated by the one and only Wayne June, and adding some special turn-based fights between chapters. I especially adore the latter. In my opinion it's a great way to make the player feel the struggle of the characters in the significant event of their lives. Plus, after each chapter, the character who just reflects on the past will receive a new skill, and can be assigned immediately. 3. Revamped Hero Skill And Path Most of the cast receives multiple skills over-haul or adding some interaction with other heroes, mainly the Combo Mark. Introducing combo adds an additional layer of thought when it comes to forming team comp. Hitting combo always comes with additional benefit, so it is crucial to choose at least two people to work together(usually one to mark enemy, the other reaping that mark). However, this is not set in stone. Each hero also provides with Path when you upgrade them in alter of hope. Path is alternative playstyle which when chosen, it alters certain skills to fit a specific playstyle. For example, Graverobber has three Path to choose. Deadeye makes her an insane range DPS; Venomdrop allows her to pierce Blight resistance and blight enemies more consistently; Nightsworn turns her intargetable all the while adding more damage and flexible position. 4. Other Compliments →Ahh, Wayne June. Your godly narration shall echo forever in my head. →Customizable stagecoach, both cosmetic and utility. →Crushing debris on the road sometimes yield good result, making the controlling the stagecoach a mini game. →The fact that any broken relationship can be fixed with excessive alcohol will never not be funny to me. Things I Like And Dislike About Darkest Dungeon 2: 1. Instead Of Clones, Individuality Stands Out The "Hiring" system in Darkest Dungeon 2 function as choose-your-fighters rather than that of the first one which is just picking from completely randomized  clones. → Like : This design fleshes out each character as important individual with stories and motive, instead of random number generator. Shrine Of Reflection is an interesting way to tell those stories. It also makes building character's specialty less RNG-based. → Dislike : Because each character is one of a kind now, hilarious team compositions can no longer be achieved in Darkest Dungeon 2. No longer can you have dual Highwayman and keep spamming Duelist Advance. No longer can you have four evasive, repelling old men on the battle field. 2. Stress And Resolve This system works more or less the same, but the result is different. → Like : Stressed-out and Resolution has been vastly tone-down to two results, Meltdown and Resolute. As a result, a stressed-out character will no longer speak death sentence to your team comp, and you have more time and opportunity to fix that problem. → Dislike : On the same note, having a Resolute character also has way less benefit to your team comp. You can no longer massively turn the tide of battle with one virtuous character. Another issue about simplifying virtue and affliction is that it removes a lot of painfully or amazingly special moment which makes the first game so iconic. Things I Dislike About Darkest Dungeon 2: 1. The True Roguelike Experience I don't think Darkest Dungeon, as a formula, work well with modern definition of "Roguelike", as in "getting slightly stronger after each encounter". Yes, you do become stronger after each region. You can get temporary buff through Inn items and upgrade your heroes' skills once with mastery points. That`s it. Other than skill upgrade, none of the buff you get is permanent. They will always disappear when you reach the next inn. As a result, it always feel like you are collecting enough resources to maintain those temporary strength, instead or slowly growing stronger. I bring this up mainly because Darkest Dungeon 2 in many ways, is trying to chase a lot of modern roguelike trends but still wants to keep the old formula which only works for relatively short, mission-based gameplay. 2. Other Complaints →Icon and its explanation should be baked in to the UI instead of a separate note you can call out. →One more full-fledged region would make multiple runs less repetitive. →Maybe it's just me, but I feel like 80% of the bosses are DPS race. →Where the hell is Reynauld?? What have you done to The Crudsader Red Hook?? 中文小簡評 →黑暗地牢續作褪去許多一代的傳統，嘗試了現今較流行的Roguelike配方，適合完全沒接觸過一代的玩家，但對系列粉絲多少有點失望。 →3D建模配上獨特哥德式畫風，別有一番風味。 →角色動作十分流暢耐看。 →音樂有種令人沉癮的旋律。 →角色故事配上特殊回合制戰鬥的敘事手法非常有趣。 →大多一代角色技能翻新，搭配新機制和技能風格，更注重團隊合作。 →先祖的配音已深植我的腦海。 →客製馬車造型及實用道具。 →撞倒路邊的土堆有時會到錢或道具，讓駕駛馬車不會太無聊。 →大量的酒精可以修復感情這點莫名好笑。 →因為角色是獨立個體，不再像以前一樣是複製人大軍，沒辦法安排派出重複角色，有好有壞。 →壓力系統精簡化，崩潰不再像以前幾乎沒救，給了玩家更多空間補救，但是這也失去了讓一代如此特別的特色。 →一代的配方套上現代Rogulike架構明顯不合。 →圖示和其說明應該要想辦法融入戰鬥UI裡面，而不是另外放在一個視窗裡。 →希望能再多一個完整區域。 →可能是我打法問題，但是怎麼感覺有8成的Boss都在拚傷害阿。

description: About This Game Darkest Dungeon II is a roguelike road trip of the damned. Form a party, equip your stagecoach, and set off across the decaying landscape on a last gasp quest to avert the apocalypse. The greatest dangers you face, however, may come from within... Featuring a completely reimagined game structure, Kingdoms is a parallel game experience to the Confessions core game mode. You will be challenged to defend a crumbling realm against incursion from all new enemy factions. Manage a persistent roster of heroes, gather resources, and pursue an epic questline in order to track down and defeat the source of evil before all is lost. Progress in each game mode is tracked separately, and you can freely switch back and forth between active sessions of either. Kingdoms is being released in thematic modules, each focusing on a different enemy threat. All three adventure modules - “Hunger of the Beast Clan”, “Secrets of the Coven”, and “Curse of the Court”- are available now! Gather your courage and ride out into the chaos of a world undone. Four heroes and a stagecoach are all that stand between darkness and salvation. Manage their stress and interaction to keep the team together until the bitter end. Nightmarish Environs From the burning Sprawl to the diseased Foetor, the long road to the Mountain will challenge your strategies and your endurance. Explore five distinct regions, each with their own unique creatures and challenges. Face Your Failures Journey to the Mountain and face down five terrifying manifestations of your weaknesses. Revel in an all new narration performance by voice actor Wayne June, a brand new expansive score by Stuart Chatwood, and bone-crunching sound effects from Power Up Audio.

reviews.text: Reviewing (mostly) every game (or DLC) in my library, part 248: ⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️☆☆☆☆ (6/10) Ngl, this one hurts. I love Klei Entertainment. I think Don't Starve is one of the standout original survival games; Invisible Inc. and Mark of the Ninja are both masterpieces in stealth; and Oxygen Not Included is a well-thought out base builder. I expected Griftlands to follow suit, and in many ways, it does! It looks great. The UI is clean. The writing is sharp. The mechanics are clever. It has heart. But it’s also confused. It wants me to care about its characters and story, but it also wants me to replay the same campaigns over and over. The problem is that the story barely changes, and the gameplay doesn't do enough to make up for it. There's a good game in here somewhere, but I don't think all its pieces quite fit together. Pros: The art is gorgeous. Klei has always had a distinctive art style, and Griftlands is no exception. The character portraits have so much personality, the environments are beautifully illustrated, and Havaria is a really fun world to look at. Even the smaller details feel considered. I love the idea of separate combat and negotiation decks. Instead of solving every problem by punching someone in the face, you can try talking your way through it. Both systems have their own cards, effects, and strategies, so negotiation isn't just combat with different animations. It's a genuinely neat mechanic that fits the setting, where getting what you want can involve anything from a good argument to a good old-fashioned beating. The writing is good! The dialogue is generally well-written, the humor works, and the world has plenty of personality. The characters have memorable designs and names, and there's a clear effort to make Havaria feel like a place with its own culture and politics. I never really had an issue with the quality of the writing itself. A ton of heart. You can feel the love behind this. Every card interaction, every character sprite, every in-world term makes it clear the devs cared. Cons: Faux roguelite structure. At its heart, Griftlands just doesn’t work well as a roguelite. The structure demands you replay character campaigns again and again, but the game doesn’t evolve in return. Characters say the same things. Plotlines don’t branch enough. Factions behave predictably. Even with procedurally generated events and random encounters, it feels like a game trying hard to pretend it’s dynamic while secretly being on rails. Dialogue bloat with little payoff. The game has a lot of text. That’s not inherently bad; this is a Klei game, and the writing is competent, stylish, even funny at times. But it rarely feels reactive. Dialogue choices often lead to the same result, and no matter how many times you interact with a character like Fssh or Borrat, their lines barely change. The game expects you to replay it over and over, yet rewards that repetition little. After two runs per character, the dialogue becomes something you endure rather than enjoy. Weak meta progression. Between runs, you earn points to unlock new perks: +3 health, +15 starting gold, a single card from a slightly different pool. It’s barebones and uninspired. The biggest incentive to replay—the character story arcs—don’t change. So when the mechanical rewards are boring, and the narrative replayability is non-existent, what’s left to motivate another run? Run length and pacing issues. A single campaign can take 2–3 hours, often stretching across multiple play sessions. That’s long for a roguelite—especially when there’s little variation on repeat runs. And pacing is weirdly structured: you're regularly told by questgivers to "go do some jobs until I’m ready," which forces you into a loop of mandatory filler. You’re not really deciding what to do next: the game is. Which jobs. Which faction events. When the next plot point will trigger. It's a strange hybrid of narrative RPG and roguelite, where neither side really satisfies. Story-driven game with no real branching. You do get some binary choices—siding with one faction or another, betraying someone—but the consequences are rarely long-lasting or surprising. There are only a few endings per character, and your route through the story is generally fixed. In a roguelite, you’d expect to uncover new branches, new outcomes, new combinations. Here, you mostly get minor flavor changes and maybe a new boss. The rigidity suffocates the sense of adventure. Underbaked systems. There’s a pet system. A graft system. Companion loyalty. Randomized map events. Influence stats. None of these are bad, but most feel like half-implemented features: introduced with promise, then left to rot. Your pet gets a few stat boosts, then sits on the battlefield. Companion loyalty can matter, but rarely affects dialogue or plot. If you enjoyed this review, please check out my curator page to find more: Verdict: Play or Pass. Also, please leave a like and visit IndieGems and our YouTube channel for more reviews like this one.

I feel like Griftlands is one of those games that if you don't like it, you're conflicted because a part of you really wants to, which is really unfortunate because the game as a whole has potential in several areas, but not single one of those areas was done well, in my honest opinion. For as much effort was put into the lore and world and as much potential as the main characters COULD have, none of that potential is met because of the game's own premise of genre. This game would've served as a better as either a turn-based RPG or a point-and-click with RPG elements. Griftlands definitely had no business being a roguelite when almost everything about it is set up for the very opposite. The characters and story are fully rigid, with the only deviation being who you "side" with halfway through each character's story. Sure, a person could argue that the characters you interact with are procedurally generated (aside from the ones involved in the main stories) to keep it fresh, but neither their names nor their personality change, and eventually, you're going to see the same old faces. All these guys could've been incorporated into a larger plot, and story drove/bonded characters you just focused more on. The sheer rigidity of the game makes for a horrible roguelite that at least tries to give the illusion of change and variety. The Deckbuilding is honestly very blase, which is a significant flaw for something that is such a large part of the game. I think they implement the specialization of either passivity through speech (which can be either intimidating or peaceful; there are some very limited situations where it will matter which you use, but for the most part, it's up to preference) or aggression through combat alright. Still, this game has unavoidable fights and talks, which can make that same specialization feel counterintuitive. I suppose you could argue this is their way of encouraging "resource management" with your cards, but that isn't exactly made until you're in that situation. I don't find either the speech or the combat particularly gripping, but I'd give the speech portion a pass before the combat. There are just too many fluff cards with no actual useful incorporation, and frankly, once you know what "works" you're most likely just going to stick with that with the exceptions of more AP and bigger damage dealers. Which is fine because there isn't really any real need for intricacy because the game is so damn short. Story is that potential part that annoys me; I have no idea why they bothered to chop the characters into subplots when none of their stories are more than 3-4 hours long (and it'll be shorter than that once you know what you're doing) and they're all fairly basic. None of them are particularly engaging on their own (though I did enjoy Hector's more for his personality and Rook's more for his implied backstory); it would've been better off being a larger plot that you could play from the characters' different perspectives using their personalities and how THEY would interact with people to help differentiate the experience of playing one or the other. The main draw from what I can tell is the artstyle (OST is fairly basic and forgettable) and some of the dialogue (unfortunately outside of main plot characters and missions you can't really have much of a conversation with anyone during the in-between), but neither of those is enough for this game to have scored as highly as it did when the core gameplay mechanics are so shallow. TLDR; Griftlands as a roguelite bad, but it has the potential for a good story driven RPG (least with this world). Hopefully, if they ever do something with this game's world again; they'll do that because I don't know what they were thinking when they mixed rigid characters+plot with roguelite.

If I had to describe Griftlands with a single word, it would be "conflicted". First of all, despite a fair number of cards, there's just two main tactics per character. It also takes way too long to get the deck do anything interesting, and there isn't much room (if at all) for crazy combos. Card battles themselves are also way too drawn out for the amount of mechanics they contain. Secondly, why does the game supposedly focused on replayability has such a rigid story with lengthy dialogues? To skip it all after your second playthrough while curbing all potential variety? As for the presentation - the art is stylish and all, but the music is forgettable at best and annoying at worst, which is quite a flaw when taking bogged down card battles into consideration. To sum it up, Griftlands is a passable experience if you want to just check out the story for each character once and then throw it into a trash bin. However, if you plan to do multiple playthroughs, unlock new cards and prestige level, and generally play the game as you would play Slay the Spire or any similar deckbuilding roguelite - don't even bother with it.

Early Access Review Deckbuilder roguelites are all the rage, and while Griftlands is interesting, it fails in the key area it tries to differentiate in: the narrative. And it's not a good enough roguelite or deckbuilder to warrant playing over other options. First, the narrative. The dialogue itself is well-written, and the character stories set up a more engaging world than the vast majority of similar offerings. But the plot isn't engaging or deep enough of its own to merit playing just to see it. That's where the world and it's myriad of characters should come in. Only, characters tend to boil down to the boons and banes they supply. I never feel like I've got major rivals or big buddies during a run. Everyone just feels like a small print number, and it doesn't really add any sense of immersion. Second, the roguelite. There's four components which slowly unlock: flourishes (super attacks that build up), perks (choose 3 per run from a growing list), mettle (passives for every run), and new cards. Flourishes and new cards are fun and unlock at a good clip. Perks and mettle especially are straight buffs that are more commonly seen in action roguelites. I think they work a lot better there because of the high skill cap that any reflex based game has. They don't work as well here and honestly just feels kind of grindy. I have no idea whether high end Prestige is balanced around it, but it's a lose/lose. Either it is balanced around it and you have to grind to do well or it's not and Prestige gets too easy. Lastly, the deckbuilder. It's very similar to Slay the Spire but with a lot more limited use cards (in the form of items). The deckbuilding options aren't near as varied as StS though, and decks can take longer to come together. The negotiation deck is neat at first but after a few plays, using it drags the pace down too much. Runs can last upwards of 3 hours negotiating with everyone (which can have some serious perks). It's too long for the level of complexity the battles offer. All in all, the progression speed, run length, and complexity are out of whack. And it hasn't really improved during EA. All that said, the game certainly isn't bad. The art, music, and sound hold up well. The fundamentals are fine enough. It just comes down to a negative recommendation when there are so many alternatives in the roguelite space that will serve you better.

At first I really enjoyed this game and the direction they took the deck-builder genre, but eventually it became a bit too tedious to scroll through the same dialogue over and over. I ended up wanting it to play much faster like Slay the Spire. Runs lasted over multiple sessions because it took multiple hours to play a single run. If you're really invested in storytelling in your games and you like Slay the Spire, then this may be a hit for you. For me it ended up being pretty boring.

Early Access Review I just finished my first play session. I was not expecting this when I bought the game. I am a big fan of Slay the Spire, and I recently got Monster Train, and I felt like that was the next step in the genre, the next move forward. The same thing, but innovated enough to be different. And then I found Griftlands. Griftlands is the new king.  It feels like a fully fledged RPG roguelike, the factions playing off each other, the bonuses for being loved/hated.  Everything you got in Slay is still present.  The random encounters.  Artifacts.  Elites.  Its just presented in a far more engaging style, almost like a single player tabletop campaign that is modular and is different on every playthrough. It feels like im playing a little bit of all the great games I love.  Moving around the map reminds me of what Hex should have been.  I get a Deep Sky Derelict feel from the combat, but thats not very accurate so I dont knwo why. I really enjoy the negotiation game play, and combat is more of what you would expect from this genre.  Not bad, not good.  But still fun and engaging with lots of different archetypes and play styles to explore. I cannot express this enough.  If you are a fan of the genre, or even tcgs in general... If the idea of shuffling cards excites you, I strongly recommend this game. EDIT: Ive reset all my progress to start fresh to play the full release.  Its like visiting old friends but none of them remember me.  (thats an inside joke)

Early Access Review This game is fantastic! This game takes the deck building, card battling mechanics of Slay the Spire and wraps it up into a fun interactive story format where choices matter. The deck building and card battles are still the core of the game. However now instead of simply following a line on a map going from one encounter to the next, there's a a visual treat of a world for the story to play out on. You'll make decisions that will matter in the game. Some of the ways decisions have impacted me are: Making someone hate me and now whenever they're nearby I suffer some penalty from them buttin' in. Someone else likes me and will help and provide a bonus. I helped someone out of a jam and every so often they send me a gift. It's also easier to negotiate with someone who loves me than someone who hates me. The love/hate status is also important in that each character will provide a bonus if they love you or a penalty if they hate you. These aren't permanent in that it seems possible that relationship statuses can change. You're also not alone in that you may have characters temporarily join your team for one encounter or a series of encounters. You can temporarily hire people and costs will depend on relationship status. You can get a pet and train them. There are also one-time rewards that allow you to summon a creature for a battle. The card battles are also fun. There's two types - battles and negotiations. I really like the negotiation card battles but I do have trouble with the keywords/concepts and what they do. I still find myself having to pause and check the arguments and what they do. It's something that I'm sure will become more familiar enough over time. One feature that I wanted to mention because I love it is that cards gain xp when played. When that bar is filled the card will evolve and you'll be presented with a choice. So even basic cards can become better over time. There's so much more that I could go on about this game. I'm just really impressed with what Klei has done with this. They have managed to take what could have easily been a mediocre "yet another deck builder" and created something fabulous. P.S. I can't believe I forgot to mention this. First, there's a panic threshold in which an enemy will either run away or stop fighting. When the fight is over you're given the choice for each opponent in either killing them or accepting surrender. For every character there is an item you will receive if you kill them. However depending on the situation there may be ramifications for choosing to kill the opponent. There's a guide that goes into this in much further detail. However it's yet another example of how awesome this game is.

Early Access Review Updated for Flourish & Mettle Update My opinion of Griftlands is largely unchanged from my original review (below). The combat is tight and you're frequently just a misplay or two away from losing a big fight, but the RPG elements get increasingly gimmicky the more you play. It's sort of sad that choosing whether to help someone or not really depends on whether the passive bonus they give for loving or hating you is important or not. At higher prestige runs then you feel somewhat punished for taking an in-character action that ends up giving you a malus - I understand that's a strategic trade off you have to make, but it highlights where the RPG and strategic aspects clash jarringly in Griftlands. My real disappointment with Griftlands though was the introduction of Mettle as an in-game currency. Hades uses a similar concept where continuous play allows you to get stronger and thus more likely to succeed at runs, but Hades uses this because Hades' game goal is to allow you to experience more story. Hades locks story behind walls for you to conquer, and giving you Darkness to boost your base character's stats made a lot of sense because you're still striving towards more story even after finishing a run. But finishing Griftlands story isn't hard in the slightest, even if you're playing at the lowest prestige level (there's also an even easier story mode). Sure it'll take you a few runs to get your first win, but once you've got there there's nothing more to see, the story's complete. It becomes challenge for challenge's sake and the Mettle just makes the challenge easier over time. Instead of teaching players to get better then you can just hit your head against the wall until you have enough Mettle boosting your base stats to give you the edge. And Hades manages to hold your attention in runs with dazzling and weird combinations that let your gameplay style shift and adapt to new quirks and patterns of combat with the power ups you get during the run. By contrast, Griftlands combat is flat and "realistic", which I still see as a big shortcoming. In short, Griftlands just doesn't benefit from the Mettle system, It feels like it's pandering to people that want its weak RPG experience without the roguelite challenge, but you could just play story mode if you wanted that. Griftland offers a cop out to actually refining your strategic skill. I just don't know. It feels like a huge misstep. On the positive, the Flourish system is well-implemented and fun without being overly power creepy. Overall, I continue to recommend Griftlands because developer, Klei, has done something interesting with the genre. However, I maintain that Griftlands does not have meaningful longevity in gameplay once you've tried out the fairly obvious strategic paths for each character. Original Review Griftlands is fun... BUT ... I do have a lot of concerns around its replayability and to explain this I need to take a quick dip into Slay The Spire. When designing a game a developer has to decide how many resources they're going to commit to various aspects of the game. Slay The Spire focuses almost entirely on the card design and mechanical aspects of combat such that the combinations of powers and card effects lead to craziness and epicness akimbo. You'll have runs where you stack armour up to 500 and drop instant one shot spells constantly, or throw an endless stream of 50 damage shivs. These things are possible because all Slay The Spire cares about is the depth of its mechanics. In Griftlands, developer Klei has split its resources to offer an RPG experience as well as a deckbuilder. To be clear, the RPG stuff is really good fun, and the way they've implemented it with the combat and negotiation and the love/hate system is sublime. HOWEVER , at least at this point in time, there's only so much to the RPG aspect of it. The quests you get shift a bit between runs, and the bosses are randomised, but you'll see a lot of what's on offer quest-wise after a few runs and I found myself skipping a lot of the quest text even after just two runs. Now, that would be fine and cool if the mechanical combat depth that Slay The Spire does so well is on par, but sadly it's just not. By splitting the game development resources to add on this (initially superb) RPG element, they've taken away from the mechanical aspect that is the reason Slay The Spire is so engaging and replayable. What's worse is they've even implemented a brawl mode where you just do the battles and negotiations in quick fire (dispensing with the day-to-day travelling and chatter) so that players can focus on the mechanical aspect, which I do think is a nice option, but I also feel it exposes the lack of depth in available strategies and wacky combinations that comparatively exist in Slay The Spire and Monster Train. To counterbalance this, Klei has tried to create different characters with very different mechanical interactions in their combats and negotiations (i.e. I think there is a greater difference between Sal and Rook than there is between The Ironclad and The Silent), which is a bold undertaking, and I would say each character's design interesting and well thought out, but, again, another large drain on design resources that, I feel, ultimately stifles the depth of development into each individual. Now it could be said that Griftlands is opting for a more "down-to-earth" approach to the combat madness, by which I mean I'm willing to believe it's a design choice that the interactions don't get absurdly out of control. You do still get fun combinations in Griftlands and they feel powerful and silly at times, but always with that edge of "if this was the real world then this would be believable" kind of approach. And maybe that more grounded approach has value, but I feel what makes the roguelite deckbuilding genre fun is the complete insanity in the strategies you can produce. Thus, if you're not going to do this kind of genre with that kind of selling point, then the RPG stuff has got to be really top notch and, again, it's good, but is it enough to make up for thinning down what I believe is the core aspect of this genre? I don't know. Maybe the compromise is for the best, but, again, do you play a deckbuilder to see the same RPG interactions? Or do you play it to make something busted happen in your deck? I think it's the latter. To be clear, I do recommend Griftlands a lot and Klei are a solid, clever developer and I want to know where they'll take the game. I think the genre combination is really cool and fun, and while I've ragged on the mechanical design being a bit lacking, I do think that people who want a lighter experience than Slay The Spire's more hardcore approach will appreciate it. However, I remain concerned that it doesn't have the depth of gameplay that the deckbuilding roguelite genre has come to be known for in terms of available strategies and the wackiness of combinations, and, ultimately, I think that's what these gives this genre its draw.

The way I would describe this is "surprisingly good". I'm not sure what it is, maybe the art style, maybe the two-deck system clearly focusing on dialogue and story way more than the average game in this genre (since I am someone who usually skips almost all dialogue and story), but for whatever reason, after getting this on a deep sale, I just sort of avoided it, played other stuff instead. I was wrong! This game is really good, and now that I finally got into it, I'm hooked! I'll cut to the chase: yes, the way this game is designed likely will kill the sort of "infinite" replayability that you get with a really good roguelike, such as Monster Train 1 and 2. However, there's a very intelligent trade-off here: until you exhaust the options, each replay will actually have quite a bit more to interest the player than the average "ok, one more" in other roguelikes. The reasoning here is the story: since there's so much focus on story, I'm sure it will eventually get stale to repeat the same events/days, since there's only so many options (basically talk or fight, with some extra variety in many situations as well)... however, right now, only 5hrs in, I've only played the 2nd and 3rd character once, and the initial character twice, and I still think there's at least one or two things I could do differently as her on a third playthrough. Simple math says I'll be playing for at least another 10 hours, maybe 15+, and that's more than enough for the price even if I never come back after that! Plus, like I said, each new game as a specific character isn't just "ok, off to fight the random mobs and bosses again!", it's "how am I going to play their story this time?" which is very cool and unique in the genre. For example, the first time as the third character, for somewhat spoiler-y reasons I won't say, I decided that he was insanely selfish, beyond a fault, and therefore used murder to solve almost every situation. I'm pretty excited to go back and recharacterize him as a f*** up who is trying his best to be better, to climb up out of his self-imposed gutter and make a name for himself in this city. This will force me to make all kinds of different choices and let me see different scenarios and dialogue (plus, play the whole game differently as this will require more of a focus on the negotiation deck). Even as someone who skips a lot of story, and I do go QUITE quickly through a lot of the dialogue, I'm actually pretty interested in the storylines here (at least in broadstrokes, I haven't seen any bad writing but I also haven't found most of the simple conversations to be life-changing or whatever, not that I would expect that). I even sometimes engage in the uncessary dialogue, the options that clearly aren't giving me hints or useful items, just to see what people say or how they act towards me. That's gotta be at least good writing since I usually couldn't care less. Anyway, oh yeah, the game, right... the game is pretty good too! I'm not sure how I feel about each character, so far it seems clear that the first one is way better at negotiation than combat, and the second is the reverse, so this does push the player towards one playstyle over the other but maybe I'm just not locking in the right strategies or getting the right random drops for new cards. In any case, I'm actually pretty impressed with some elements of the gameplay too, for example I like how, while you can find card upgrades as rewards, all cards can automatically be upgraded at the end of battle once you've used them enough. I was also getting worried that there wasn't any meta-progression, but now I have new outfits and a special store specifically for meta-upgrades, and a perk system... To be honest I can't really think of anything this game does "wrong" except that the art style isn't my favourite (for people, it works quite well for aliens and robots!). I guess it can be hard to get money / really make a specific build? But this game isn't really about that, it's about following a story and making choices along the way. I guess my only real critique is I've played for 5hrs and I still have almost no idea what is happening during the negotiations. Sometimes I add stuff to their orbit, they add stuff to my orbit, it feels like if I just do "damage" a lot and put up my shields a lot, I win... so I've been winning a lot so I must understand it, right? Except I don't, a lot of the time I either take or do damage I wasn't expecting, and I did lose once because of that, so I guess that part of the game could be less complex and/or more clearly explained and/or have better signposting and tooltips. Still, it's been fun to learn each of the three styles, for both negotiation and combat, and I'm having enough fun to easily excuse one myseterious loss. All in all, if you can go into this with the right mindset, and generally like deckbuilders, I think you'll have a blast (that mindset being: this is not a wall of floors and random bosses to hit your head against over and over until you finally win, this is a choose your own adventure book with a very good, or at least decent, card game that functions as the glue between events and the reason for things happening or not happening). Especially if you see a sale, buy it! And to be honest, if I even play for 10hrs, I've paid more money than the full price here for less fun than that before. Give it a chance! So far it doesn't even have any like IdPol bs either despite the focus on the female character in the art, it's just good ol' fashioned steampunk noir sci-fi style goodness!

This game seriously needs its flowers, I have never played anything more addicting and enthralling in my life. Everything from the setting, to the mechanics, to the art style, and to the music all coalesce to form something truly unique. I haven't played many deck builders, so some elements may not seem so innovative to me as they are, but by god it feels like there's so much thought put into the inner workings. I feel like this is properly seen if you try to engage with its achievements, the game encourages for you to find its exploits and discover all of these interesting synergies that you'd otherwise never think of without them in mind. Each character on their own boast a wide variety of tactics at their disposal and it never feels like the game cheats you out of victory if you have a well-polished deck. The storymode, brawl, and daily challenges are such fun ways to interact with all the niches and that's further expanded upon with all of the cool workshop content I've experienced. It doesn't feel like this game receives much attention by the wider gaming community, but the love is here all the same and I'm glad to be a part of it.

Early Access Review 1、目前版本不自动适配语言。进入游戏，【OPTIONS】，【OTHER】，【LANGUAGES】向左两次到简中，【APPLY CHANGES】切换到中文。存在lua崩溃闪退问题，我不知道怎么办，期待大佬或者官方支持。 2、在Epic买过的可以免费领Steam版本。 3、目前版本没有云存档，多设备玩家需手动同步。存档和模组默认路径：C:\Users\<USER>\AppData\Roaming\Klei\Griftlands\。已经消失的存档，除非修复硬盘找回文件。《欺诈之地》单次冒险流程很长，死掉的挫败感很强，死前可以ESC回到主菜单重新读档。可以每天开始的时候手动备份一下存档路径/saves/...下面的文件，必要时粘贴回去读档重玩当天，或者体验其他剧情分支，不需要重启游戏。 4、Epic和Steam存档分开，复制粘贴就能继承。只想复制收集进度的话，只复制...\profile.lua一个文件。 5、Steam右击游戏【属性】添加启动项【--dubug】进开发模式。开发模式功能很多很杂，谨慎使用！测试频道有实验版本，玩腻了可以感受新版本。 6、嫌进度慢的可以适当改文件，或者用存档投降刷，但可能会【破坏游戏体验】，慎用！我只收集到95%的角色，还在施工中…… 7、感谢官中！质量有提升空间，我做的版本汉化了45%的卡牌和大部分界面，仅供参考。官中修复了几次，目前影响游戏的有：【黑石的恩典】只回3不是10，变体规则（突变器）【至多拥有3个宠物】，萨儿4费【压碎】给自身减费……卡牌错误还有不少，不过忘记了……对话和界面另说吧，工作量挺大的。 8、可以自己做本地化。打开游戏路径\data.zip，按路径解压出\localizations\zh_hans.lua和.po，把文件名和文件里的zh_hans全部换成zh_diy或别的，.lua的id改一下不重复，name改一下可以中文，这样就在游戏里就能选了。汉化内容都在.po的msgstr下面，建议用Notepad++编辑，记事本要另存为保持编码。Poedit虽然专业软件，但是有未知问题。如果你想完善汉化，我很乐意分享现成的python代码帮助校检。 9、Klei提供模组的早期支持，坐等大佬们把各种MOD摔我脸上。狂喜！ 去年Day1入手的老菜鸟分享些和游戏不直接有关的东西，希望有用。

description: About This Game The Choices You Make, Make You. Growing up in humanity’s first extrasolar space colony means navigating a new world full of wonder, danger, and beauty. Explore the wilderness, study, fall in love, discover strange creatures, and deal with the consequences of your actions. Your choices will directly affect the lives of your friends and the fate of the colony. What kind of world will you help make? Will you survive to enjoy it? Why do you remember doing this before? Growing Up on an Alien Planet You have your whole life ahead of you. Will you spend it studying in school, or diving into the intriguing flora and fauna of this new world? Will you introduce space-age technology, or live in harmony with nature? Will you battle massive beasts, or nurture future generations? Realized in brilliant watercolor, the world of Vertumna is yours to explore. Your Pasts and Your Futures Matter Everything you learn and experience will make you and your colony stronger. You will thrive and you will make mistakes. These formative moments - your memories, decisions, and friendships - become collectible cards you carry with you. Each season brings new obstacles on Vertumna. The battle cards you earn from your experiences give you new options for overcoming these challenges, whether that is navigating relationships, learning new skills, exploring the planet, or staying alive. Every decision counts, during this life and the next. How Many Lives Will YOU Live? The cosmos is full of incredible mysteries, and your ability to remember your past lives is one of them. There are dozens of different endings to your story. How many lives will it take to save both your colony and the planet? Are you ready to wake up again? Features: Use memories of past lives to explore 800+ story events. Discover more than 250 battle cards as you grow up on an alien planet. Play your best hand in challenge encounters to ace your math test or escape from a wild snapbladder. Make friends, fight with your parents, go on dates, fall in love, and save the colony. 29 wildly different endings based on the choices you make each month. Pick from 25 colony jobs, like goofing off as a depot clerk, or surveying the valley. Grow into 15 skills, including bravery, toughness, organization, and empathy. Get to know 10 dateable characters, including dog-boys, aliens, hot politicians and stone cold killers.

reviews.text: Incredible First Impression, Fumbles Badly at the End The first four hours of this game are incredible, with great art, writing, music, and an engaging twist on deckbuilder gameplay that isn't too difficult but also encourages you to play optimally. The story is compelling and surprisingly dark; it takes some big swings and doesn't shy away from the consequences of living in a new colony on an alien planet. All of that changes after about the 2/3rds point, though. The random events start to repeat, the overall plot becomes strained and disjointed, huge world-altering character storylines are introduced and resolved in a single short story segment, the card game becomes trivially easy even on hard mode, the list goes on. There are three issues that stand out to me as particularly egregious: It takes so long to actually enter into a romantic relationship with any of the characters that, by the time you finally do, all of the activities you can do that give statistical rewards and consistently result in interactions with them are useless. And even if you do do an activity for no mechanical progress, very few if any of the events change based on your romantic status (or if they did, it was impossible for me to tell that they did). You can explicitly interact romantically with your partner, but there were only two scenes for who I ended up with-- one of them repeated five times. By a similar token, the cracks in the activity system really begin to show in the last few years. I maxed out the activities in the engineering lab and did a smattering of other activities, but when I went to do other activities the writing would be... off. Either the events would have the adults communicating with me as if I was a child, or they assumed familiarity with character interactions that I just never saw, etc. The ending was incredibly unsatisfying. There was obvious social and political upheaval imminent, the yearly alien attacks hadn't been resolved, we hadn't secured a stable food source, etc. But instead of addressing any of those issues I just got a specific epilogue for my romantic interest (wherein we broke up after a couple years, then they worked themselves to death... ) and a generic "and everyone else lived happily ever after" and an invitation to play through it all again. There's of course tons of content I didn't see, and I can see how some of the things I didn't explore could address some of these issues-- but based on discussions I've seen and how fundamental some of these flaws were I have no desire to play through this game again (let alone 28 more times to get all of the endings, if this ending was any indication of the general quality of them). But despite all that I can't stop thinking about this game-- the characters, the world, and the art are so compelling and it makes me so sad that the ending soured me so much on the experience.

Warning to ppl that wanna buy this game for the romance, visual novel aspect: You gotta break up the existing couples to romance them lol. Doesn't matter (SPOILERS!) if you were their bestfriend or if they were your secret admirer , they end up with someone else. Even when they are coupled they flirt with your character, and there's only one character I've seen that is ok with poly so wth is this. Dialogue doesn't seem to be any different as well, nothing referencing anything except a small part and some tiny crumbs. This department of the game is pretty weak anyways, compared to something similar and a modern release like Arcade Spirits 2 or Boyfriend Dungeon. That being said, there's honestly not a whole lot of "romance" in I Was a Teenage Exocolonist to begin with. I bought this game mainly because I saw cute alien pets. And I wish you could get more cute alien pets. I got two pets with my almost fully maxed out stats in my first playthough. They don't do much except add stats to your card deck. Even then you have to equip them in your "gear". There's very minimum interactions with the cute alien pets too, but you can pet them so I guess I got what I was looking for? Game wasn't at all what I expected honestly, there aren't really 50 different endings, there's like three that matter. I played the demo in its entirety before buying and read some reviews--this is what pulled me in! I was expecting more, the demo (1st year,) started off really strong! But the rest of the game is same-same, you know when all major events are gonna happen, and because of all this, the gameplay is predictable. I finished IWATE in 3 hours and yes, I read the dialogue. I already started another playthrough of the game and I gotta say, it's not much different, other than the flashbacks (SPOILERS incoming!) and now you get to save people that died. You also meet some new people in your second playthrough. Anyways, this is the only part where choices actually matter. Choices only really matter in your second+ playthrough when you know when and what is going to happen and you have the ability to change that. (This makes the gameplay even MORE predictable.) So reviewers were kinda lying/false advertising, choices don't matter if you are playing it for the first time. (Should've expected such from beta testers...) In fact, most of them are locked or not there at all in your first playthrough. I was a Teenage Exocolonist is one of those games where the ending you get in your first playthrough is not going to be the "true" ending. (Like the Zero Escape franchise) And honestly, this game has too little replay value to do something like this. And personally, it's a little too repetitive for me to play a third time (2nd time already boring and getting more cute alien pets ain't enough to convince me at this point tbh), let alone my 50th time. The card game in IWATE also gets dull and easy quick. (It's simple rounds of one or three, you gotta combine card power to match the goal amount or higher, you can use 3-5 cards depending on situation.) This is pretty disappointing to me because I was looking forward to the card game. Wish there was more flavor to it. The card game is also the main "gameplay" of IWATE unless you change it to the coin flip (based on your stats) lol. But why would you do this, everything you do in the game gives you card stuff. If anyone's looking for card-based rpgs, this isn't it. If you're looking for a relaxing game. This isn't it either. There's literally impending doom around every corner. Edit: Just wanna make myself clear for ppl interested in IWATE, this isn't a joke. The game uses LOSS as a main motivator for all the characters including the MC, it is also what drives the plot. This is one of the content warnings of the game. (There's more in the game menu and on the game website.) I just wanna mention this, the "loss" can be sudden or take place throughout years. It might be difficult to deal with for some ppl playing the game. (And SPOILERS!) All deaths/losses are unavoidable issues for first-timers. Most of the losses, if not all, become avoidable in your second+ playthrough. Imo, this is at the cost of personal development of the MC and other characters. Learning how to cope with loss is arguably the main theme of the story and this might not be for some ppl simply looking for a cute, colorful and fun game to relax to. I Was a Teenage Exocolonist is kinda like a sci-fi Growing Up or Chinese Parents. The music is great, the artwork is unique, the setting is cool, just not what I expected from the story and RPG elements. It's lacking in those departments tbh. It's also $25 and the two games (four if you count the first part of my review, 7 if you count the Zero Escape games lol) I have previously mentioned are cheaper, have more depth, and offer character customization (did I mention that IWATE has no character customization other than a feminine and masculine slider?) and I dare say more replay value even with the 50+ multiple endings this game offers. They also all have romance. No cute alien pets tho, so that's a loss. Edit: Refunded this game after writing this review. I realized it's totally not for me even though I wish it was. Mechanically wonderful, the story is engaging, the endings make my heart ache (not in the best way) Without spoilers: I had been eyeing this game for a while, and the first few hours were a blast! *The card game aspect is good, it's challenging when it needs to be and not annoying the rest of the time, fairly balanced and the art for the cards is great. *The story took me by surprise, especially during my first run. The replayability aspect is there if your focus is the story, and certain important events are made easier once you "solve" them for the first time (which makes repeating loops way less tedious, I'm thankful for that!) *The stats you need for certain choices never felt wrongly placed imo, I encountered some events where I couldn't do anything too special without certain stats but it doesn't significantly hurt your progress. If you're able to raise your stats and pick those options you do get rewarded, so that part feels fair as well. MY ONLY ISSUE: The story doesn't wrap up as nicely as I'd expect, given the work you put in for certain endings. It feels as though I've given it my all, and still some things just happen that leave me unsatisfied. **heavily censored spoilers here** There's what I assume would be the "best possible/ good" ending where you negotiate peace with the aliens which took me some effort, certainly more than my first 2 endings, so I expected it to make life in the colony all better. Which, it did, with the exception of the romantic aspect. The goal of the game is to explore your choices, and try to live different lives to then achieve a better result than last time. In my case, I wanted to go for Dys as my partner. And HOLY COW, I FEEL...lied to??? I felt as though the story wanted to convince me to push past his negativity because we were both the outcasts and supported each other. And then put effort into resolving the game's conflict at the same time, to have a happy resolution as a reward for my efforts and planning. In the end, no matter what I do, no matter how hard I try to cater to either him, the colony, or the aliens , or all at the same time, the relationship just ends up crumbling when he inevitably, in every ending related to him, leaves. And this isn't even just Dys, relationships with other characters have equally disappointing things happen down the line. TL;DR / closing thoughts I like the themes of the story, how it makes you put in effort for the rewards, and how some conflicts are just meant to happen while you can change other outcomes. If you want to focus on the story of the colony and help it thrive (or not) the game is wonderful and I 100% recommend it. BUT if you want to ALSO enjoy a romantic story where the ending feels rewarding for your time and effort, this is not the game for that.

!! Spoilers for some early events, how the player can affect them, and discussions of the game's romances !! This game has a lot of moving parts. It's ambitious, you can see that from word go, and it is, overall, competently executed. I love the visuals, the character designs are distinct, I have this weird fixation with min/maxing in life sims so I can see myself coming back periodically just to see how high I can get my stats by the end of the game. It's a good way to pass time, the sole minigame's simple but satisfying(it does start to feel stale after a while, but I took that as my sign to take a break). But I felt like I saw a lot of cracks after a few hours. The story and world don't feel meaningfully reactive, it feels like it's running a bunch of binary yes/no checks. For example, in my first playthrough I chose Tammy as my character's childhood best friend. MC's mother and Tammy's father both died, they had a shared history, high affinity, and MC found her crying due to grief. MC cried with her, but the fact they both lost a parent within, like, a year wasn't acknowledged. I'm not saying the game should have pivoted the scene to focus on MC's feelings instead of Tammy's, but it felt jarring to be talking about grief without mentioning that. I expected some level of commiseration, either MC saying "hey, I get it, I just lost a parent too" or, given Tammy's personality, that she would've asked how MC was feeling and tried to shift the conversation to *their* grief. But that would take time to write and program, so instead the game checks if Tonin is alive then runs one of two conversations. It just makes the world feel flat, and, unfortunately, the game's full of moments like that. You pick MC's childhood best friend, but that doesn't affect anything outside of how many affinity points they start with. It sounds like a goofy thing to complain about, but since you start off with a cast of 7 kids, you'd think they'd chat about that kind of thing, especially as they become teens and start to drift apart(I could see a lot of angsty "we never hang out anymore" conversations, particularly when dating comes into the mix). You also choose an augment for MC, things like unnaturally good eyesight or an extremely calm temperament or extra fingers. Other characters have augments, too, and they're huge parts of their personalities. But not MC's, their augment adds a card to the minigame deck and increases a stat at the start, that's basically it. I didn't see it mentioned by other characters at all during dialogue or flavor text. So, sure, the game lets you choose from a bunch of options, but it rarely feels like it matters. Save Tonin and he immediately retires, you never see him again. Save Eudicot, she acquieses to Lum and effectively bows out of the story. Save MC's mom and her sprite stands near their dad's on the overworld. I would have preferred a few options that actually have an effect on things instead of a bunch that don't. Maybe choose one character to be MC's best friend and just let the player define what that means, how their relationship formed and developed early on. Nem would've been a great choice, she could've been the outgoing extrovert who pulls a shy MC out of their shell or raised hell with a more mischevieous MC, icing them out regardless once she starts grieving. It also would've given the player a reason to side with Helios outside of "this is a game, nothing matters and I want to choose the cartoonishly authoritarian option". And it could've added more weight to the opening cutscene once it loops back around. Give players a set parameter(their best friend, their special quirk) and let them define what that means to them(whether it draws them out of their shell or reinforces confidence, becomes a crutch or is written off). As it stands, MC just doesn't feel like a part of the gameworld. They desperately need a more reactive element to ground them in it. Relationships, platonic and romantic, suffer the most there. I never believed any of these characters were into MC except Rex, and MC/character friendships are never acknowledged outside of affinity checks. MC always feels like a second choice for romances(again, except with Rex) regardless of their affinity with any given character. Cal and Tammy are obsessed with each other and difficult to split up. Marz and Tang aren't actually interested in relationships, although MC can still pursue them. Dys will always have a crush on an alien. Rex and Nomi can form a cute triad with MC, romancing Rex alone results in some weird moments with Nomi but is overall sweet. If you want a monogamous relationship, it's gonna be a lot of work and a little luck, plus it very well might end abruptly and unsatisfactorily. I understand relationships don't always work out IRL, people aren't always compatible, I'm totally cool with MC getting shot down by a character(Serafen my beloved...) but it ultimately just feels like MC doesn't need to be there. MC/character relationships also aren't acknowledged unless you fought to break up a couple. MC's parents don't have any thoughts on who their only child's dating, Marz' dads don't have a moment with MC if they pursue her. In general, characters outside the main cast don't feel like part of the world. They're mentioned in passing, you almost never see them, the overworld's empty except for romanceables and MC's parent(s). Having minor characters randomly crop up and give us short scenes to help flesh out the colony would've been nice. Instead, they're just numbers. 100 people live here(you will see a handful of them), 17 people died, etc. MC really feels like they exist in a vacuum. Yes, because they're the special-est kid in the world, they can change the outcome of the story, they can choose who lives or dies, but nobody really seems attached to them and whether or not someone survives barely matters. The epilogue's brief. It doesn't talk about anyone outside of MC's immediate circle, just their partner(s) and parent(s). It would've been nice to get a line or two about what other characters were doing. I'm not saying every character needs a post-ending novella, a simple "And Cal, who you hung out with a couple times, took over Geoponics eventually. He's happy/sad about life in the colony" would've been enough for me. On a game that sells itself, partially, on replayability, a shallow relationship system and unsatisfying endings make it kind of hard for me to recommend. Like I said, it's pretty and I could see myself checking the "skip seen dialogue" box, turning on a podcast, and trying to speedrun it for various endings, but I was ultimately disappointed in the game overall. It had its moments, it's not like it was unplayable or I'm kicking myself for spending money on it, I just thought the experience as a whole lacked the depth a project like this needs to shine. EDIT: After reading a few other reviews I feel I should mention that the progressivism is ultimately a thin veneer. It posits living in a post-racial society where humanity's past mistakes are hammered into kids' heads(good! I like that) but concepts like white supremacy or the realities of assimilation never come up. We never really get to hear an argument against cultural assimilation. Beyond that, the only black character you're likely to see is a fierce independent girl who sees everyone as below her, and there's a hyperintelligent stoic East Asian girl with a fiery temper. The text itself furthers racist stereotypes, regardless of the writers intentions. Combined with their unwillingness to acknowledge real-world racism in the text, some design and writing choices feel disingenuous if not slightly insidious.

I'm a chap in his late 30s who's played a LOT of video games over the years. An hour into playing this game turned me into a bawling, blubbering mess - like no video game ever has.
