I bought this on the current (fairly large) sale as of 8/25/23 and just sat down and beat it in one sitting. Well, I got an ending in one sitting, about 5 hours. It's 4AM now and I am riddled with existential dread in a way that I haven't been in a long time. That alone should be a pretty good indicator of the writing in this game, but I am going to spoil a bit below this for ONE of the many many endings because its made me think a lot, and frankly if you aren't scared of a single ending of like 50 being spoiled, I would maybe give this a read. At the start of the game, the character I bonded with most was Nem. She was this happy, sporty, bubbly kid which is just how I was when I was a kid. You do the activities you are good at in game and so we did sports and rough-housed together. As time passed and we grew up sports turned into guard duty for the colony, and down the line we both joined the military. The colony started to get a lot more scared, of everything. Nem wasn't as happy anymore. She broke up with her abusive boyfriend and we started dating at the end of the game, and this is the part that scares me. I kinda ignored the rest of the colony for the sake of trying to defend it and keep everyone going. I indexed heavily into my friendship with Nem, so I wasn't really good enough friends with anyone else to try and save the colony another way. My parents were dead, Nem's brother was dead, a lot of people were dead. The final 2 years in game I spent more or less just performing the military duties and talking to Nem here and there. Nem was tired and slowly becoming a husk of her former self, barely acknowledging me when I talked to her at some points. The other colonists minus a few I remained friends with, hated me. I was a braindead military bro that had joined up with the invaders that took over the whole place. I was a traitor. In my mind at this point, though, the only way to save things was to fight our way out. I didn't have the skills in game to do it any other way. Well, I did it. At least, as far as the game is concerned, I did it. I got the war hero ending, where Nem and I survived, and the colony lived on. Nem and I had 2 kids in the epilogue, and we both died in our early 30s in the line of duty. This was not something I was prepared to face at 4am after pushing to finish up the playthrough, but I got that ending and thought to myself, "Wow, what a horrible way for things to have gone." The characters I didn't manage to save, the life my character wouldn't get to live. Even though its a successful ending where neither me nor Nem died in the game and we were happy until our epilogue deaths, was that really happiness? Its possible that could just be the short epilogue driving me up a wall a little bit, simply not giving me the full satisfaction I want from an ending, but it could also be the way they intended it to feel. Bittersweet. Games like this terrify me, to be honest. I typically look things up at some point so I don't ♥♥♥♥ it up in dating sims, and this definitely isn't that. I feel like I've lived a life out in 5 hours, truly. Thats pretty horrifying. Whats scarier to me is that it made me think about my own life, the ways that I've been treated, the ways I've treated others. Conversations I did and didn't have. Relationships I do and don't have, all based on my own choices in life. The fact that this game and its writing were capable of making me think this deeply about my own life and the way that I have ended up as a 20 something... Yeah, I'd say its worth the price of admission. I honestly don't know when I'll play this again and go for another ending. I dont know if I ever will. I'd rather not get another bout of depression and horror at 4am thanks to a narrative hitting really hard lol As far as how this holds up as a game, there's a lot of reading (duh) and the card mechanic can get a bit tedious in the endgame, but its pretty engaging throughout. Anyways, I'm gonna go and think about my life choices now :)

Product received for free Disclaimer: I was a QA tester on this game and have put hundreds of hours into it across multiple platforms. I was not asked to write this review and there was no expectation I would. I just genuinely adore this game. I Was a Teenage Exocolonist is a rare type of game that presents a narrative of both breadth and depth  and then allows players to explore that narrative through repeated groundhog's day scenario replays. There are over 600,000 words in the Exocolonist script, but you will only encounter maybe 1/8th of that script or so in any one playthrough. You control Sol (who you can name whatever you'd like), a man, woman, or non-binary character who grows from age 10 to age 20 over the course of the 10 years that a single playthrough of Exocolonist entails. You will decide what Sol does every single month during this 10 year period, including where they work, who they hang out with, and defining your version of Sol's opinions and beliefs through hundreds upon hundreds of dialogue choices. The game combines a Princess Maker style character progression system with a very compelling and emotional choice-rich narrative and card battles using cards which represent the many memories and choices your Sol has made. All of this together creates a surprisingly reactive system that encourages you to roleplay as a different Sol each time you replay. Through narrative choice you will be able to define everything from who Sol is attracted to and where they work down to the very granular level, such as whether or not Sol eats meat, what they think about the way the colony is run and which factions within the colony's web of characters Sol supports. And that's only the start! There are 10 dateable characters, each with their own story arcs that can end in any number of ways, and a vast array of secondary characters with their own arcs and often surprising backstories, many of which hold a further level of depth to them if you really go digging into everything this game has to offer. I could go on and on about the incredible aesthetic of the art in this game (I love Exo's future clothes!) and how fun it is to watch these characters grow physically alongside their narrative arcs, or gush about the emotional and stylish synth soundtrack, or Vertumna's incredibly vibrant ecosystem, but instead I want to talk about another reason why Exocolonist is always going to have a special place in my heart: Most sci fi depictions nowadays are bleak. Dystopias have become the norm in our cultural representations of the future, and for good reason, as our present day reality is itself quite the dystopia. I Was a Teenage Exocolonist does not follow this recent tradition. And that's not to say Exo's vision of the future is at all naive or happy go lucky, either. Instead it does something far greater and gives you a rich and conflicted future in which characters are free to express themselves and to live comfortably in that expression, but there are still those who would like to take away that freedom out of fear, malice, or misguided attempts to help others. Exocolonist's future is beautiful and scary and awe-inspiring and most important to me, it gives me hope. It thoughtfully presents a future different from those I've encountered before and then fills in that world with an incredible level of care and detail so that you can live in this world for as many groundhogs as you'd like.

This game is good, but it really needs a primer, so I will give you one now: You will likely miss the entire game if you try to do everything. You really do need to commit to raising relationship with a couple of characters and spam them with gifts as often as you can to max them out, this isn't like Persona or Potionomics where you can easily see everything in a single playthrough. Also go exploring often, even to places you've already been, that's where a lot of the plot is hiding. Primer aside, it's a well-written game with a focus on relationships. It's like Persona, but with the novel conceit that you play a character from age 10-20 and very slowly grow up over the course of 20 or so realtime hours. It's also very queer, with nonbinary characters, a full playersexual cast of romance options, an ace/demi character and more.

description: About This Game The Cosmic Wheel Sisterhood is a thought-provoking narrative experience from the creators of The Red Strings Club. Featuring a richly diverse cast of characters, Tarot-like card creation, divination, and a branching story that spans time and space, The Cosmic Wheel Sisterhood explores themes of identity, community, and personal responsibility in a beautifully hand-crafted universe. You play as Fortuna, a Witch living exiled on an asteroid who forms a pact with a forbidden creature in the hopes of regaining her freedom. Reconnect with your Witch friends after a 200-year-long exile, meet new Witches, and use the cards you created to pierce through their pasts and futures. As you delve into this universe, you will see yourself immersed in the complex web of interests that surround your coven, leading to a political plot that will define the fate of the Cosmic Witch society. reviews.text: Edit: Turned comments off, got very annoying getting 3-4 notifications a day from escaped 4-chan users that everyone that plays this game or reads this review is a soy-consuming something or other. Review remains unedited, just turned the comments off. (This review is spoiler-free) So, I'm a run of the mill, heterosexual, cis-gendered white guy. I do not believe in astrology, and I do not believe in tarot. Normally, I don't think thats an important detail to add to any kind of review, but I feel thats an important qualifier to justify my claim that the writing in The Cosmic Wheel Sisterhood is strong enough that despite the fact that I have no direct point of commonality with the characters in this story, it completely resonated with me. Thats not to imply that if there isn't a character you can directly connect an aspect of your persona to that you can't enjoy a story, we all do it all the time. This is, however, a game focused on a very diverse cast of (all women by nature of who can be a witch in this universe) omnisexual intergalactic witches. All this to say; I'm not exactly the targeted demographic for this game lol But, often times in games that focus on story, or just with writing in general, there isn't the extra level of prose there to elevate said story above its base merits. You can feel the perspective of the writer and thats definitely an important piece to experiencing literature, but writing something that goes beyond an individual experience or perspective is a pretty hefty task and most stories, especially when it comes to video games, fall short. That is not the case here. Through the almost 7 hours it took me to beat the game I was continually surprised at the depth each of the characters seemed to have. It makes sense in a narratively driven game that the characters would be fleshed out, but the way that each of them mingled with the themes present in the game was actually very impressive especially compared to a lot of this game's contemporaries. It felt like they all had tangible goals and aspirations that required attention. It didn't feel like people just popping in through your window on a stranded rock because the writers made it so, but it felt like real people searching for answers despite the cosmic setting. Good writing is really, really rare in games, especially the larger you go with audience, because frankly a lot of people don't have the time to sit down and be narratively entranced, sometimes you just wanna go shoot some stuff in Halo. That being said, if an entrancing narrative is what you're looking for, you've got a good one sitting right here. I was intrigued from the demo back during Steam Nextfest, and I'm glad the full game delivered. There was a very, very small team behind this one and the creative choices they made to allow for a strong and wide spanning story to come to life despite the limitations of their team are just kickass. Reading the cards and fortunes remained pretty intriguing every time I did it, and only got more interesting as time went on through the game, it really felt like you were both in control and at the whim of the cards which is a delicate balance to write. The way that player agency was treated is extremely interesting as well, and while it is not the same at all it did remind me of the way Kentucky Route Zero approached player agency, and thats genuinely one of the best stories I have ever experienced in a video game format. As far as some minor demerits, I did feel as though the romantic relationship you are offered felt quite rail-road-y? Is that a word? Either way, the way that the character just kinda showed up and it was like "Hey, you're in love now!" was pretty wonky to me. I was trying to be careful up to that point to ensure that I didn't accidentally romance someone and was pushing to help one of the characters I liked to see where I could trigger the romance route and uh... I don't think that you can romance anyone but the one character I ended up with. I'm not positive about that, but I'm fairly certain that was my only option. Its not the end of the world, but in a game about a bunch of horny gay witches I was kinda surprised how limited that route felt. Without spoiling as well, there was a shift in the second half of the game that felt... weird. I did end up enjoying that shift but it was definitely surprising and it felt like an odd tonal change for about an hour or so. You settle into things pretty quickly but it was definitely one of those where I went "Oh, okay this is happening now". There's also nowhere to fit this cleanly but the art, aesthetic and soundtrack are just 10/10. Seriously the music makes this game, it does so much heavy lifting for setting the mood of some scenes. I follow the composer (@thefingerspit) on Twitter or X or whatever its called now, and they were posting snippets of the soundtrack leading up to the game's launch. Absolute bangers throughout. Cosmic Wheel Sisterhood isn't just about whats on the surface, horny witches vying for power and trying to stay true to themselves. Its about the friendships and bonds that keep up standing when sh*t knocks us down, and there's a really beautiful story here. I really enjoyed this, and honestly its a damn shame that it came out in a year that is so absurdly stacked with GOTY contenders because I feel like this would be getting more attention that it deserves were it not sandwiched between Baldurs Gate 3, Armored Core 6 and Starfield. I'm hoping that this quirky indie title finds its space in the cosmos that is Steam, because it deserves some love. If you're interested in it, I say give it a go. Ah, The Cosmic Wheel Sisterhood. Deconstructeam never fails to hook the player with a truly interesting idea. In Gods Will Be Watching, it was non-linear, non-chronological story that routinely presented the player with a multitude of tough decisions. In The Red Strings Club, it was managing a bar, mixing some drinks and talking to all sorts of different people, while getting to know the outside world through their eyes and perspectives. And in The Cosmic Wheel Sisterhood the main draw is the premise itself. Following the journey of an exiled fortune teller, living on a lonely (albeit cozy) asteroid, crafting your own deck of cards and helping a plethora of weird, charismatic characters. Good news is, everything that makes Deconstructeam games great is here and almost better than ever before. Wonderful pixel art, astonishingly good music courtesy of Fingerspit. The dialogue is written in a very natural, believable manner, while also remaining fun, entertaining and sometimes deeply emotional. Card crafting mechanic works very well and never becomes tiresome, even if the editor could use some more quality of life improvements. What can i say? It's just fun to tinker with your deck, meet other witches and sort through their problems, while coming to terms with your own. The Cosmic Wheel Sisterhood instills an expectation of a very personal, dark, but ultimately hopeful experience, where emotions and introspection are the heart of the story. And yet... It doesn't really pan out this way. It's disheartening, but this is probably the first time when i didn't get what exactly a game by Deconstructeam was trying to tell me. The Cosmic Wheel Sisterhood starts as the story about sisterly bonds, witches, mortals and the infinite cosmos. About desperately trying to care for the things you love in a cold, uncaring void. But in the last third shifts its gears so suddenly that you can physically feel  whiplash. Instead of building on the established emotional core, the game becomes a rather dull and simplistic management simulator, where you need to run a political campaign. Send your comrades to do various tasks, study graphs, self-promote, that kind of stuff. There's absolutely nothing wrong with it on paper. Deconstructeam always liked to spice things up with some small vignettes that offer dramatically different gameplay mechanics. Each situation in Gods Will Be Wathcing was a game in and of itself, while the most memorable moments of The Red Strings Bar happened outside of the titular speakeasy. Same thing happens in The Cosmic Wheel Sisterhood, as flashback scenes usually carry the most emotional weight, even though they are basically dialogue segments without any gameplay. Unfortunately, the moment you reach the campaigning portion of the game, the fun stops. Mind you, it stops in more ways than one: while the mechanics of managing the campaign are fairly dull, the story stops making sense as well. The whole last third of The Cosmic Wheel Sisterhood feels like it was shoe-horned into the game for literally no apparent reason. It doesn't try to tell you anything new about politics, it's not drawing any coherent parallels to the real world crises, it does not force the player to make any difficult or meaningful decisions. In other words, it contributes almost nothing to the narrative, while also detracting from what made the earlier portions of the game so good. Sense of melancholy, bittersweet reconnection with the loved ones, discovering new people after literal ages of isolation and loneliness. Yes, Deconstructeam was always vocal about its interest in social politics and gender issues, but that is not the problem. It never was. The problem is, the devs are not saying anything particalrly fresh, worth listening to or challenging in any way: it feels confusing at best and needless at worst. The studio dedicated a good fraction of the game to discussing politics of a fictional society of space-faring immortal witches, and the player has no skin in the game whatsoever, because there's no attachment. They also show a rather traumatic scene from a life of a trans woman... Only to then handwave her problems away with some magic. And you, the player, are left wondering what exactly you were supposed to get out from this whole interaction. Meanwhile, there's a whole cast of quirky, interesting or just weird characters sitting on the bench, mostly collecting dust. On that note, the story practically self-destructs at the very end thanks to a rather interesting, but pretty problematic plot twist. Without spoilers, it does make the player question their decisions, sometimes horrifyingly so. However, the twist also casts a big shadow on virtually every other plot point, which can result in a laughably nonsensical culmination. Honestly, The Cosmic Wheel Sisterhood tried to do significantly more things that it probably should've. The story strives to be both personal and profound, but, much to my sadness, succeeds in neither. It was a bit too ambitious while having no clear, or at least understandable, message underneath. Still, i do not regret my time with the game: even an underwhelming Deconstructeam manages to be one of the more memorable releases of 2023. It's just a shame it will never become an instant recommendation like The Red Strings Club.

The Cosmic Wheel Sisterhood starts out amazing with incredible pixel art, great music, and a really fun custom card-building mechanic. The story about isolation and connection feels deep and emotional in the beginning. However, the second half loses its way. Changing into a political management sim ruins the pacing, and the romance feels forced. More than that, the political message completely misses the mark. By saying men cannot be witches but non-binary people can, the game excludes men while basically treating non-binary people as woman-lite. For a game that claims to be inclusive, it feels hypocritical and preachy instead of welcoming. It is worth playing for the art and early story, but it falls short of its real potential.

After 12 hours of game play, I have to admit that I cannot in good heart recommend this game. I really thought I would love this game since I love occult-like games, tarot, space, and anything with witchy-aesthetics. The fact I was able to make really cool tarot cards out of different sceneries and arcana was already a win for me. The characters looked interesting, the art style is super charming, and the story at the beginning was very catching. If that is enough for you, I would say this game is good for one play through. But this game fell short with so many misses. The story itself is disappointing..."Shape the fate of the cosmic Witch society" makes it seem like your decisions matter, right? Well, I would go look for something else such as Oxenfree (if you have not played this game, you totally should!). As a good majority of these negative reviews states, the choices you make seem to matter until you find out mid-game that they don't. Some do, but they are minor choices that don't really affect the story. Also mid-game there was a huuuge shift in tone. It goes from light and fun, to something that felt rushed and heated between the MC's friends which didn't seem to fit their characters. Throughout the whole game there was so much salaciousness...don't get me wrong I'm no prude and enjoy sexual interactions and exploring sexual desires between characters in books/games (and fully aware the correlation between sexuality and witches), but with almost every character bringing the subject up its so disorienting and completely takes me out of the game. It was funny at the beginning, but came up in conversations with characters where it felt totally out of place. The character movement speed is atrociously slow and didn't even realize that you can spam-click to get her to go faster until I was doing a second run to try and get 100% in achievements and seeing how different the ending was. THE REPLAYABILITY IS NOT GOOD....for a couple of reasons: new game plus-like function & skipping text. Nothing is really new about the dialogue when you play a second (or third if you really want) playthrough unless you make different choices (minor conversations do change), so why not skip? Nope, you have to spam-click to get through dialogue. Secondly, it would have been amazing to be able to reuse the card designed you did in a previous playthrough. I mean why not, the main premise of the game was to create your tarot cards and you spend a good amount of time actually making them look nice. I found myself in my second play through, not being interested in the attempt and rushing to select my arcana and scenery. Thank you for reading my rant! Have a lovely day.

SPOILERS!! READ AT YOUR OWN DISCRETION I tried to be as vague as possible but yeah. This game had amazing potential. The story telling in the demo got me hooked enough to purchase the full game to play, as a woman, someone with a sister, and someone who has experienced depression there were multiple moments in this game where I cried. I liked the game play of making cards and loved learning about people through them. Then the game violently pivots and rushes storylines that could have been really beautiful. My first experience of this pivot is when one of the characters abruptly confesses they are in love with you. They act weird the whole time you talk to them then they confess and you confess back and suddenly you're in love this is great and everything is perfect... it's jarring and weird it feels completely unnatural and forced. Your wish was for romance not sudden deep committed relationship. You have better chemistry with other characters yet this one is the one you end up with? Not to mention that if you don't pick the right answers they will end up betraying you at the end with no warning as they are coded that way. The other rushed storyline is about a trans woman. The idea behind this storyline is super interesting and emotional. but that's all this felt like, an idea. You could feel the story behind it but it was like they condensed it down into just the most important parts and left out the details. This could have been something bigger, and I was left wanting more out of this character. Then we get shifted into a political party management sim??? This outright threw me for a loop. Suddenly we are no longer talking about emotions, making connections, and learning about characters. Instead we are using the knowledge to manipulate the outcomes of the game. To make this worse it is honestly against what our main character stands for. The game becomes very management style as you have to keep telling people what to do, they do it and come back, and then you send them off again. It gets boring, the story loses meaning and starts to completely unravel. Your choices feel like they have no meaning and the conversations are just dull. My last issue with this game comes from a political standpoint. This game was sold as something that was LGBTQ+ friendly/supportive. However a huge issue comes up when we meet the transgender character, while her story is very emotional and beautiful we then get insight about how "men" cannot become witches yet non binary people can. I am not sure how I feel about this as I don't think we should be putting nonbinary people into the box of women. I don't think this information was integral to the story line, even with the trans woman's story included, and felt like it was thrown in there as a bone to the community and honestly comes off as disrespectful. In the end I feel like the game had a lot of potential if it kept it's focus on the storyline and people instead of becoming more of a political party management sim. It also should have been slowed down as a lot of the stories feel completely rushed. I really liked the first half of the game, it's a shame it didn't end as strongly.

I hate this. I really wanted to like this game. I adored Deconstructeam's other games such as Gods Will Be Watching and The Red Strings Club. This game had me going for 4/5s of it. The card making parts are fun, the decisions you make have some major impact on the game. There are even some amazing and touching progressive stories this game tells. Even the change of pace that takes place in act 5, where you are on taking a stance on witchy political views and campaigning for them feels really good to play out and takes your earlier games decisions into account. Then we get the final act and... everything just explodes. Everything you've done feels so completely ignored, and you're forced into a unsatisfying situation with several characters acting completely out of their nature. Even putting that aside, the final scene is one of the most frustrating moments I've ever had in gaming. Even if you make several questionable, even out of character decisions to get on to the path of a good ending, one wrong click, or in my case, asking a question at the wrong time without thinking that it would be a game ending decision (especially when throughout a play through, the game repeatedly prompts you to confirm major decisions in earlier acts), and that's it, game over. You've just wasted 10 hours. The game's autosave feature kicks in, starts you over fresh and there is no way to go back without playing it all again. I adored so much of this game, but an unsatisfying final act and a "got ya" final scene feels like crap. And with no way to pause and go 'hey wait, that isn't what i meant game, let me load a prior save', due to the autosave feature, you feel the game cheated you.

This game feels like a visual novel with resource management bolted on. The UI is missing many quality of life features that make playing frustrating such as being able to change your mind about worker allocation before ending the day or being able to easily see how many/which people have negative status effects. There doesn't seem to be an option to save mid-day, so I would have to either finish the whole day or lose my progress. I encountered at least two bugs. After loading a save point, some of the dialogue boxes disappeared. They reappeared after starting the next day. I have a super ultra wide monitor, and the text in dialogue would sometimes fail to fit on the screen, so I couldn't read it all. Some scenarios related to resource management don't make sense. For example, an emergency could occur at mid-day or at the end of the day requiring people to help, but if you already assigned workers to nearby tasks like shoveling coal or doing an interview, those workers would be unavailable to deal with the emergency because you cannot undo allocation decisions... I am left thinking "I guess someone just has to get frostbite because I can't interrupt an interview happening 20 feet away..." Another example is being unable to hold a feast if there isn't enough food already in the pot. I had plenty of food in cans, but since it wasn't already in the pot I couldn't use it to deal with the scenario. At least one mechanic never seemed to be explained properly. Some workers have special attributes (e.g., ice savvy) that seem like they might affect their work performance, but if that's the case it never seemed to make a difference to me, and I don't think it was ever explained in the game. The resource management system was too unrealistic for me and seemed to encourage a play style that felt like cheating. For example, sailors who are sick due to not eating can get better by simply spending time with the surgeon without needing any food to solve the problem. The cure to starving is not surgery... You should not be able to substitute a doctor visit for not eating. The game has some positive points, but for me they don't make up for the UI issues or counter-intuitive resource management. The characters and story are interesting, and I did make it through to the end of the game. There are a few cutscenes with great audio or visuals. The conflicts between key characters are well written.

First, the good. The art & music are beautifully made and the characters really come alive on their own. The bad on the other hand, makes this something I cannot recommend as a game. Generally speaking, the issue is how segregated gameplay is from narrative. As a narrative-driven game, it is simply jarring to encounter situations where your crew start falling into despair while food, heat and decorum are all at maximum. Examples of cases where the story and gameplay elements fall apart are simply too numerous to count. As for the narrative choices, the game quite simply, allows you to lie without consequence. For example, there is an option to use a recently-caught leopard seal for a feast for your crew. However, upon selecting the option, the leopard seal in your inventory isn't consumed, while the rewards for setting up the feast is immediately applied. More gross lies involve telling one crew member that you are siding with them, and then immediately telling another that you are in fact not. As such there are no consequences of any sort when it comes to lying to your crew, as they seem to simply not be able to converse with one another about what you just told them. There are also a number of incredibly jarring and illogical narrative choices towards the end of the story that don't really provide any sort of meaningful benefit despite being incredibly inhumane. It simply does not make sense why these options were even provided at all. Overall, the game feels cool to play at first glance, but quickly grows into feeling......lacking. Lacking in realism, lacking in the difficulty of survival, lacking in narrative logic, lacking in character motivation and most of all, lacking in gameplay-narrative cohesion.

This game does some things well, and others poorly. Pros: - The characters and dialogue are competently written. It's not a masterpiece, but it's solid and consistent, with different characters having very distinct personalities. - The artwork in general does a good job of selling you the fantasy of a rugged crew braving the elements. - The game system for assigning crew members to different tasks is easy to understand, but surprisingly deep. Cons: - The simulation aspects of the game are fairly poor and detract from your immersion in it. For instance, if you spend enough fuel to keep your crew's morale up, you can go through the entire game (40 weeks or so) without ever providing any food to your crewmembers, which is jarring. - The resource card system is needlessly convoluted and very buggy, which makes it a pain to work with. - The deal-breaker for me, however, is that this game doesn't respect your time as a player. Like how in Week 11, it killed off one of my crewmembers because of a casual dialogue choice I had made in the prologue. You want to fix that? You need to start the game over. There's another one of those events that caused me to restart the game, by week 30 or so; I was close to finishing the game, but then I got screwed over and felt I had to restart. Also, there's no way to skip forward dialogue, which makes replaying segments a chore.

The game is a lot of fun, great narrative and atmosphere. However there are some criticisms i have in regards to the general design and play experience. I'll give a bullet list and then go in depth on some problems i had. Pros: - Great storytelling - Very nice atmosphere - Fun survival management Cons: - A lot of clicking through repeated dialog, could use a skip or fast-forward for parts you've already done (EDIT: patch 1.2.2.0.0 Fixes this as you can hold ctrl key to fast forward dialog) - A branching decision tree type load system that doesn't work with the survival mechanics and isn't focused around clear 'decision points' - Research points.. they don't do anything. - A few UI bugs outstanding So to talk over the cons listed. I found that my experience was that i played my first run, got game-overed a couple of hours in, and then had to start from the beginning because my issue wasn't any one particular decision made, but rather just not having known how to optimise resources from the beginning. This meant that i had to click through a huge amount of text that i'd already seen just to reassign some rations differently next time. From what I've seen this is a common issue, and leads into the other major criticism i have. The game uses a branching system for loading your save, the implication being that these points are where you can make different decisions to effect your run. BUT, that's not really how this game works at all. Being a survival game the major thing you're fighting is gradual erosion of your supplies or loss of crew, and that isn't an easy load back to fix. This usually means that in case of a game over you have to load a long way back and not just to the last "decision point". This combined with the fact that there aren't really branching narratives so much as a couple of different but very similar outcomes towards the end mean that your decision tree is just one or two game overs and then a straight line to finish once you learn how to optimise resources. Not only that but because the game doesn't really have much in the way of a branching narrative there really isn't any motivation to come back and try something different at certain points either as you'd be clicking through so much repeated dialog until either hitting a game over or reaching the ending. Finally the research points are inconsequential, I've asked around and it seems they give you a +1 to a specific dialog ONLY if you don't have enough loyalty, making them almost entirely meaningless in the game. This is rather silly given that they require allocating workers and sacrificing resources to obtain, and are never really clearly explained. Ultimately i really like the game, but i think the branching load system was a bad design choice, and exists purely for the sake of metaphor (somewhat ironically). The core survival system and narrative are very fun, but include some weird additions like research points, and game overs unfortunately make it so you end up having to repeat huge segments of text until you're no longer having fun. All love to the devs and definitely not trying to be a negative nancy, but thought i'd express my honest thoughts.

The good thing about this narrative manager is that it's not terribly hard — games of the genre, like Help Will Come Tomorrow or Gods Will Be Watching tend to be, they often revel in the feeling of "you WILL fail and get an imperfect ending, that's the point of suffering." Not The Pale Beyond: I saved everyone on my first playthrough and was close to a perfect ending. Not that it was trivial and mindless. The difficulty is balanced all right, if slightly on the lower side. I do feel that the game would benefit from being slightly harder. On the other hand, the game has insufferable bugs. 30% of the time interfaces would glitch and either refuse to let me assign people and resources or not show it. You can usually go back and try again, but it gets really annoying. Quality control also begins to falter by the end, with missing punctuation and pieces of dialogue missing (I think). The Pale Beyond is just, overall, shoddy and rough around the edges. There's no getting away from this. Some things happen or not happen depending on your earlier choices without you knowing. But the writing is good, and that's more important. You follow the story of a small crew that gets stuck in ice and needs to survive until rescue amidst falling temperature and morale, hunting penguins and seals for blubber and meat. The crew is just big enough to allow for some sacrifice, but small enough for you  to remember every sailor — so they're not mindless pawns you throw around missions. As for the main characters, leaders whose loyalty you need to win and whose stories you follow, they are a mixed bag. I liked some — like the doctor whose changes you get to see (and influence!), or a distrustful illiterate carpenter-poet. Others have left me scratching my head. A cook who only every talks about food? Really? It's like a fat kid from an 80s movie whose only personality is being fat. Still, even if some of the characters are misses, none are annoying, so slowly winning their trust and helping everyone survive is fun. As for the ending... either I'm missing something, or it's kinda underwhelming. The idea with magic peaches that let you change the timeline — i.e. rerun the game for better results is less fun and ludoharmonious that the developer team thinks. I don't feel like this game needed this particular fourth wall hump. But overall, I recommend The Pale Beyond . It's just the right size, it doesn't pull big "gotchas" on you, it's beautiful and has a great theme. What more is there to ask?

Do you remember the faces of the people that died because of you? He asked me. Every single one, I answered. He was right; it's not the choice that is difficult. It's living with the consequences. I wasn't sure what to make of The Pale Beyond, at first. The closest game I'd compare it to is This War of Mine, but make no mistake - this is a very text-heavy affair. And the way your choices weave into the gameplay, the character dialogue, and the general direction of the story? Oh, let me tell you about that. If you've played Disco Elysium, you probably remember how impossibly impeccable its script is when it comes to adapting to what you've said and done; how some small remarks can almost turn into arcs that develop and resolve in a satisfying manner. Well, here it's perhaps not as expansive, but it's still the same amazing feeling. Listen, Robin: they will remember what you said. Whether you stay true. Who you chose to help, why, and how exactly. It never feels like you're just exploring a dialogue tree, and it's never obvious which dialogue option will do what. You need to intuit it. Feel what really makes your crew tick. Can you do that, Shaw? But then there's the... issue. A really big one. It's almost enough to make me reconsider my recommendation. Almost. See, the game's resource system pretty much expects you to sacrifice something, and then to regain it later. Which is fine - but it never mentions that. Your very first playthrough is pretty much bound to end up in a disaster because of mistakes you commited a long time ago. To avoid spoiling anything and being too specific: it's okay to sometimes not give enough. The crew is hardy, Shaw. As long as you care for them, they'll be fine; they might complain at the moment, but you'll find ways to appease them again. Calculated risks are an absolute must - especially earlier on, when things are... less deadly. Now. I'm sure there's a question going through your head. Is... is it possible? Can you...? And the answer is yes. You can. But some sacrifices must be made. Painful ones. Ones you might not be able to live with; but you'll have to. That, my friend, is the true meaning of leadership. There's one more thing, Shaw. One of the endings provides you with a, shall we say, revelation. It's one of those that don't hit very hard at first. Only after a while, after you thought about it for a bit. It fully solidifies this game's central theme as "sacrifice". For what, you ask? Well, what will you sacrifice for, Robin? Listen. It's late. I need to retire for the night. I'm certain you've heard enough, and your mind is already made up anyway. Bring them home, Robin Shaw. Curator page

I'm partial to survival games, but they often come off as cheap and unpolished. But, so far, The Pale Beyond shows an impressive amount of consideration. Thoughtful, branching conversations, excellent music and art. It's very moody, and very well written. Easy to get lost in. FINAL UPDATE, having now completed the game. Gameplay balance is challenging and well thought out. You'll find yourself thinking about how to overcome the seemingly insurmountable odds even when not playing it. That said, it is remains balanced and this is a design and narrative accomplishment. "What's the replacement rate on my fuel?" "How many penguins is it gonna take to not starve to f'in death over winter?" The tension is real. There are some minor glitches and nuisances still left in the game, particularly in the latter half (ie med bay being unavailable due to narrative events, etc which can necessitate resetting a day) but it's all tolerable. Some bugs are about the only thing that is not immaculately polished. Final issue, I do agree with other reviews that the ending, while amazing and satisfying, does arrive missing a bit of background. I would recommend to the Dev to do a bit more play testing to tie up loose ends here in a more narratively cohesive way, like they've done diligently throughout the rest of the game. (ie I never made those choices, so why is this under discussion? Did I miss something?) That said, the pros vastly outweigh the cons here. Overall, I'm very impressed. One of the best survival games I've played. When the Devs make another game I'll be first in line. If a well written, well designed, atmospheric, survival game sounds like your cup of tea, don't miss The Pale Beyond. Cheers!

description: About This Game Five years ago, The Viscount and its crew set sail through The Pale Passage in search of absolute magnetic South. The ship and its crew were tragically lost to the ice, never to be seen again. Her sister ship, The Temperance shall follow in her path, hoping to find answers where The Viscount failed. A polar exploration game set in an unforgiving frozen wasteland where you embark on a treacherous voyage across the ice and through the Pale Beyond. It’s a stunning yet harsh landscape that can change at any moment. Every decision matters and the ice doesn’t care. As the expedition unfolds and the Polar Winter approaches, every decision you make will have a meaningful impact on the story as you navigate your way across the ice. You didn’t ask to lead this expedition, but here you are. Stuck in the ice, Captain missing, miles from civilisation. Someone has to take charge. Manage your meagre resources, balance safety and morale, make the hard calls, and head in the only direction you can - through The Pale Beyond. Keeping the crew (and sled dogs) safe, fed, and warm during the expedition is imperative. Surviving the ice will matter little in the face of a mutiny. Every vote will count. So keep the crew on your side. Featuring original musical compositions, shanties and accordion tunes that will dynamically evolve alongside your journey. The team is interested in exploring novel systems-based narrative games that combine the kind of deep choice and consequence narratives you find in interactive fiction, with extensive systems more common from other genres - all designed to bring in-depth worlds and characters to life. reviews.text: 🎮 The Pale Beyond 简体中文个人汉化补丁发布！ 《The Pale Beyond》是一款很棒的南极生存叙事冒险游戏，可惜一直没有官方中文支持。作为一个很喜欢这款游戏的玩家，我自己做了个简体中文汉化补丁，分享给大家。 汉化内容： - 25,000+ 条对话和叙事文本已翻译为中文 - 主菜单、设置等 UI 界面也做了中文化 - 角色名和船名等专有名词保留了英文原名 使用方法很简单，通过Github下载压缩包 → 解压到游戏目录覆盖 → 启动游戏就是中文了 GitHub 下载地址： https://github.com/RandolphVI/ThePaleBeyond_Chinese 我也用这个汉化补丁录了一期游戏实况，大家可以看看实际效果： https://www.bilibili.com/video/BV1T8XrBbEQT/ 基本上对话和界面都能正常显示中文，基本够用。如果觉得有帮助的话，欢迎给这篇评测和 B 站视频点个赞，也方便让更多想玩中文版的朋友看到~

先说结论：我非常非常喜欢The Pale Beyond，它将【资源管理】和【故事情节】两个要素结合得恰到好处。 简单说下剧情：在这个虚构的世界观中，人类的科技大约处于现实中19世纪初的水平，这是一个科学与探险精神同时飞速发展的时代。玩家所扮演的角色Robin Shaw应聘成为一艘【蒸汽+风帆混合动力】的南极破冰探险船Temperance上的大副（仅次于船长的职位），去寻找五年前失踪在南极地区的另一艘科考船。此次探险由一些匿名富豪资助，甚至连Temperance都是他们出资提供的。然而，冒险的真实意图不为人知，主角意识到这艘船上藏着许多秘密...... 比如我们亲爱的船长先生从一开始就认为这是一次有去无回的旅程...... 游戏开始时，船上一共会有27人左右的船员。我起初以为会很难分清谁是谁，但在和每个人交谈之后我发现并没有这样的困惑，这就是我最喜欢本作的一点：它强化了【剧情】在游戏中的分量，让每一位船员都有自己的故事和特点。比如天赋异禀的女摄影师、脾气火爆的总工程师、自命不凡的地质学家等等。玩家在游戏中要做出很多选择、权衡利弊，但也有很多对整体剧情影响不大的对话选项，船员们也各自有许多不同的应对。巨大的文本量使得本作成功地塑造了很多人物形象，也会在游戏后期成功地将大自然带来的恐惧和绝望打入玩家内心。 本作中所能支配的几种资源是“士气”“燃料”“食物”“船员”和“雪橇犬”。在游戏序章部分（约前1.5小时）没有太多【资源管理】的要素。在序章之后，整艘船会陷入一系列危机之中，此时就会考验玩家的资源分配能力了。我不再详细说明这一部分的游玩细节，因为与其他同类型游戏是相似的。 缺点方面，UI有一些bug会影响到正常游玩；并且本作英文文本量较大，需要玩家拥有较高的英语水平。 ------------------------------------------------------------------ 以上是早上刚买游戏的时候写的，现在是晚上10:47。我居然真的花一整天通关了本作，上一次我这么干可能还是一年前。现在我可以用一些朴实无华的语言来确认一点：这真的是一个非常好的游戏。 ------------------------------------------------------------------ 跟开发人员沟通了一下关于将游戏翻译成其他语言的问题。我说可以免费提供本地化工作，对方表示之前没有考虑过这个事情（因为游戏文本有至少30万词，跟个小说一样），所以现在做出来的游戏成品非常难以翻译成其他语言，这可能跟什么后台代码有关吧，我也不太懂。总之大概率是不会有官方中文了，大家或许可以等以后民间的汉化组...

description: About This Game Pyre is a party-based RPG in which you lead a band of exiles to freedom through ancient competitions spread across a vast, mystical purgatory. Who shall return to glory, and who shall remain in exile to the end of their days? Key Features: A New World From the Creators of Bastion and Transistor Experience the biggest and most imaginative world yet from Supergiant ! Get to know an ensemble cast of characters struggling to earn back their freedom as you make your way across the forsaken land called the Downside. Action-Packed Three-on-Three Battle System Battle against a colorful cast of adversaries in pitched, high-stakes confrontations where each victory (or defeat!) brings your exiles closer to enlightenment. Choose three from your party for each Rite, and outfit them with mystic Talismans and powerful Masteries. A Branching Story with No Game-Over In Pyre , you will never be forced to lose progress. Whether you prevail or you fail, your journey continues. The interactive narrative is expressed through a story that no two players will experience in quite the same way. Challenge a Friend in Versus Mode On top of the single-player campaign, Pyre features a local two-player Versus Mode, where you can play against a friend (or CPU opponent) in one of the game's fast-paced ritual showdowns. Form your triumvirate from more than 20 unique characters. Rich, Atmospheric Presentation Pyre once again showcases the award-winning talents of the team that created Bastion and Transistor . From the vibrant hand-painted artwork to the evocative musical score, every aspect of Pyre 's presentation draws you into its fantasy world. Accessible, Customizable Controls and 4K Ultra HD Graphics! Play with gamepad or mouse-and-keyboard using fully customizable controls custom-tailored to PC. The game offers a highly scalable challenge both in the campaign and Versus Mode. Experience it all in stunning 4K resolution (compatible display required)! Unlock 'True Nightwing' Campaign Mode After Finishing the Story Complete the Campaign, then go at it once more, 'ironman'-style, with a unique set of rules, higher stakes, and greater challenge! We hope you'll be surprised and delighted by the result, and that the many characters you’ll meet and stories you experience during your journey stay with you for a long time to come. reviews.text: This review is 100% spoilers free and discusses why some people did not like the game. Some Supergiant's fans gave it negative reviews, I disagree but understand their point of view. First of all I would like to address that Transistor is my favorite game on Steam and Bastion is not far from there. I spent +60 hours in each one of them and absolutely love them. Supergiant Games however are famous for creating a totally new and differenet experience in each of their games, going from action RPG to mostly strategy and finally to some weird visual novel party based fantasy sport. I expected that Pyre would be different than the other two but some fans did not, they expected Supergiant to do their famous gimmick in which they blend the story telling in the middle of the gameplay. I personally believe that Supergiant should not be stricted to a system just because they perfected it and were famous for it, they might try something totally different (which they also perfected here with Pyre as an almost visual novel) . I can understand why they want Supergiant to stick with their old system but that does not justify the negative reviews on the game just because of its genre is visual novel and did not use the same gimmick as the previous two games. Pros: + Amazing story which you can dive into as deep as you are interested. + Memorable unique characters, you might love some of them you might hate the others but in the end they're all interesting which creates the connection between you and them. + Do I even need to talk about the soundtrack? Darren Korb kills it again here. + Art style is absolutely gorgeous and developes an awesome atmosphere that pulls you into the game, in my opinion one of the best arts in video games by far. + The core gameplay (The Rites) is a lot of fun with great character differences and variety of play styles. You might find it too easy at the beginning, well, wait and see how the game can give you a good challenge if you're willing to accept it. + The RPG elements in the game are important and highly customizable, whether it's the items or chatacter upgrades. + On a technical level my mind is blown by how the story goes by with the decision making and your wins and losses. It's like every and each player will get its very own different story than the other. I played Telltale games and The Witcher but this one stands out among them as the highest number of possible results you can get. Like even in some major choice matters I found that my options were totally different than my friend's because of how we approched the game and our relationship with the Characters. Cons: The cons in my opinion does not affect the enjoyability of the game but just to mention them. - I personally do not think this is a con but some people might be bored with the too much reading in the game and that is why I stated that Pyre is close to be a visual novel. So if you hate reading a lot of dialogues this might not be the perfect game for you. - The core gameplay (The Rites) could've taken more parts in the story since each match lasts only like 4 minutes, that is not something annoying or negative in the game I just think it could've been a little bit better. - My only take on Supergiant games is that they should've mentioned how Pyre is close to be a visual novel so that their fans who played Bastion and Transistor can understand the major changes happened here, in other words the game description is missing some elements. Overall: I find Pyre to be one of the best games I ever played so far especially in terms of story and choice matters. The characters are strong part of the game and influence your choices a lot. The soundtrack and art style are on a different level. And last but not least the core gameplay is well thought and really entertaining and much deeper than what you think which most visual novels don't usually devolop. For those Supergiant fans who did not like the game, I can understand your point of view but does not mean the game is bad just because it does not use Bastion and Transistor's gimmick, or because the genre is not your cup of tea. Thanks for reading.

This game is truly completely different than all the other Supergiant games. I’ve played for a while now, and I believe the following points are important to know about Pyre. 1. The game is extremely story centered. You have to read a lot. If you don't like reading dialogues or anything at all in games then I think this game is not for you. The game depends on you reading everything. The story is interesting though. Sometimes there are really funny moments. All in all it’s not boring to read it. 2. You have to make many decisions, and yes they do impact the story to a certain extend. Some have more impact than others though. 3. So, expect for the fights, this game is like a Visual Novel. The most time is spent reading. The story is interesting and I want to know what happens next. Also the characters. Those are so diverse and likeable; it’s nice and refreshing. The art is just gorgeous and the music is too, just like in any previous Supergiant games. I personally really like reading a good story so I'd definitely recommend this game to anyone who does too. --- I've written a little bit more about story & characters below (light spoilers) --- Story I‘ve read a lot of Visual Novel’s (not sexual one’s, mind you) and I also read a lot of books. I think the story is interesting but not as engaging as it should and must be as a Visual Novel’s. There is a whole backstory written in a book about the Rite’s that you are completing, which you can read. It’s mostly told out of the perspective of a person, but it still gets boring fast. Sometimes after completing a rite, I gained up to 8 pages of this book at once. It’s not fun reading 8 pages at once. I do believe there is a better way of implementing the backstory into a game. I really wanted to read it all, but it began feeling like a task all too soon. Of course, this could have been me being lazy. Characters I love the diverse and likeable characters that Pyre presents to you. In fact, I like them so much, that sometimes I ask myself: Why can’t we speak more with them? Instead of having so much text written in a book, why not be able to deepen your friendship with your companions? I did ‘care’ about them a little bit, even with the relatively short and rare interactions that are available. But being on a journey with them, being a team, completing the rite’s together… I think it would have been good for the game if there was a possibility to speak and interact more with your companions. But that’s really just my opinion. Obligatory German: ‘I’m sorry for my bad English’ and thanks for reading! :)

Like my reviews? Go follow my Curator page. Something I believe I should note right off the bat is that Pyre is not a game that will appeal to everyone. Even if you're a fan of other Supergiant games, do your research before you buy this game. That doesn't mean Pyre is bad. No, it's the direct opposite of that. However, compared to their other games, this one might be harder for some to enjoy due to its heavy visual novel elements. Now that that's out of the way, I think the one word to describe how I felt after finishing this game is awestruck. Even if this is a more niche title, it doesn't change the fact that Pyre is one of the best games 2017 has to offer. Graphics By Supergiant standards, this is the best they've done in the visual department. While all of their games look great, this one was eye candy from start to finish. All of the different areas really set the tone, and the character designs are extremely diverse and unique. There isn't much to say here, but there isn't anything about the graphics I can fault. I don't think there's any way they could've done it better, because the game is absolutely gorgeous to look at. Gameplay Pyre's weakest aspect is its gameplay, however it's not bad at all. At worst, there was a lot of missed potential, but at best, you have an extremely interesting and unique take on football/basketball. There's no denying that Pyre's gameplay is extremely unique, and it's extremely fun. It's not completely polished, as certain characters like Ti'zo and Fae/Dae/Bae/etc. are ridiculously OP, but the concept is there and it works. I loved experimenting with the different playable exiles and adapting to the fairly dynamic (and constantly exciting) Rites, and the game encourages flexibility. That being said, the Rites themselves don't actually get all that interesting until about 1/3 of your way into the game, where more gameplay options are provided to you. It's quite understandable if you find yourself slogging through the first part of the game. But once you get passed that, the gameplay becomes far more complex and interesting. Also, it's important for me to mention, this game has awesome online multiplayer potential. I was surprised to hear this game didn't have online multiplayer, because the Rites are very enjoyable once you get through the beginning stages. Overall, the gameplay's still good, but definitely where Pyre falls short. Story Pyre's story made me feel a wide range of emotions. At some points, I was getting teary-eyed, and at other times I was audibly yelling at my monitor in excitement. It felt like a real journey, and it was so fascinating to watch all of these problems unfold and see how the characters respond to it. But that's where Pyre is at its best - the characters. I loved every single one of them. Every single Nightwing who joins you is fleshed out and three-dimensional, you can tell plenty of time and care was put into making them lovable. One thing I also liked is that the game did take certain character clichés and flip them on their heads, one example being my favorite character, Rukey. The way he's portrayed at first gives you the vibe that he's going to be a shady, self-centered, and annoying prick who will want to make you bash your head into a wall. Instead, without getting too much into spoilers (but I'll censor it anyway just in case), Rukey turns out to be an honest and supportive person who cares deeply for his family's well being. Anti-trends like this are pretty common with all of the characters, and it made me love everyone, even the exiles you face off against. Pyre is probably one of the most deep and open-ended games I've ever played, with there being a ridiculous amount of lore and ways for the game to play out. It's definitely going to overwhelm some, but if you power through it, you will find that this game is very immersive and keeps you on the edge of your seat from start to finish. Audio Supergiant games have always had a great soundtrack to back them up, but they went above and beyond with this game. Each piece feels different and fits their intended tone. There wasn't a single piece that felt out of place. The songs with vocals, however, were the highlights. Darren Korb and Ashley Barrett have beautiful voices, and every time they sang, I got goosebumps. While some might be disappointed by the lack of Logan Cunningham's normal narrator voice, the one they had for this game fit the theme a lot better in my opinion and I was perfectly fine with him. This game's narrator especially got more entertaining as the game progresses, although explaining why would lead to spoilers. To conclude, just like the game's story and visuals, I can't find anything to fault here. Replayability The amount of replayability in this game surprised me. There's a LOT of different outcomes to the game, and with the incredible story, I'm considering going through it again just to see what other interactions I can find between the charming ensemble of exiles. It's a shame that the game doesn't have online multiplayer, though, otherwise I would be even more hooked on this game than I already am. Verdict Although Pyre is most certainly unique and an incredible experience, I think a good game that it can be compared to is Undertale. While Pyre isn't a 10/10 game and some people will find the visual novel aspects tedious, both games have extremely well developed characters, an amazing storyline from start to end, and soundtracks where every single song is enjoyable in their own way. Supergiant has given us yet another high quality game, and if it appeals to you, dear Reader, you will be more than satisfied with this incredibly brilliant and enthralling emotional rollercoaster. Graphics - 10/10 Gameplay - 7.5/10 Story - 10/10 Audio - 10/10 Replayability - 8.0/10 **PERSONAL PICK** .:9.1/10:.
